speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reference to the papers brought down concerning the Canadian Northern railway, on page 14, there is a statement of the earnings of the road for the year 1913, and an estimate of the earnings for the years 1916, 1917 and 1918. It would be important if the Government could get from the company a statement of the earnings for the year 1913 up to date, and an estimate for the balance of the year. Since we have an estimate for the year 1916, perhaps it would be possible to get a similar estimate of the earnings for the year 1914.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will be very glad to ask the company for that information.

Referring to the dssuments brought down yesterday in connection with the Canadian Northern railway, at page 5, there is a letter from Sir Wm. Mackenzie to the right hon. the Prime Minister, in which he says:
S*or the reasons mentioned in the memoranda and statements respecting the Canadian Northern Railway system, submitted-
I do not see where these memoranda and statements appear in this book, as they do not appear to accompany the letter. It would be very important that we should have these.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Everything that accompanied the letter has been brought down, and the selection of the documents printed was made by my hon. colleague from Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). I have not examined the blue book very carefully. The documents alluded to were placed upon the table of the House. My recollection-I am not absolutely sure of this-is that what appears on the following page 'is a memorandum setting forth certain documents and information which were required from the company. When the company handed in these documents, they placed a copy of the written requisition which 'had been made in front, and these which follow in this book were the documents alluded to in the letter. That is my impression at the moment.

Apparently that letter of Sir William Mackenzie was accompanied toy some memoranda which explained the reason and the necessity for asking aid. I cannot find in the book or in such of the papers as I have looked at any such memoranda. If there is any such it should be in possession of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The memoranda consisted of the information which was demanded to be furnished on two separate occasions. I do not know whether the information supplied on both occasions is printed in this book because I have not had an opportunity of examining it, but I do know that the information in a somewhat extended form was supplied on two different occasions. I will make inquiry and perhaps I can inform my hon. friend privately.

speechtext: On motion of Hon. G. E. Foster (Minister of Trade and Commerce), Bill No. 170, to amend the Canada Grain Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
In the working of the
terminal elevators, the grain that comes in is burdened to some extent with freight and other charges, necessary to convey it to the terminal elevator. The warehouseman has, under the Act, to pay these charges when he takes the grain in, and these charges are then repaid by the shippers of the grain either before or at the time they ship out. In the course of the working of our own elevator we have had to pay out in the course of the half season's operations money for freight amounting in gross to seven or eight hundred thousand dollars, but this is almost immediately recouped and deposited to the Credit of the Receiver General. The purpose of the first section is to carry out the idea of the Auditor General, which makes it unnecessary for us to get a vote for an amount, the maximum of which we do not know, and it enables us to draw for the money that is necessary on the Consolidated Revenue Fund, the money to be paid back again to that fund. When the internal storage elevators are added in operation to the terminal elevator at Fort William, the amount of these transactions will Ibe much larger. Last year I had to get an advance from the Auditor General, and the advance was repeated and repeated. By this Act we. will avoid the unnecessary loading up of the Estimates with large amounts, and do away with the necessity of asking the Auditor General for advances from time to time.

When this Act was in
Committee the minister promised us certain information with regard to the handling of grain at the proposed interior terminals, and also the rate that would be charged for the service to be Tendered, and generally to give the House an idea as to how the Government proposed to operate these interior terminals.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The interior terminals
will be operated in very much the same way as the terminal at Fort William. These interior terminals are meant for the storage of grain. The grain before being stored has to undergo the operation of grading. It is sampled, inspected, graded and taken care of in the elevators exactly in the same manner as it is at present taken care of in the terminal elevators. This is the first and primal reason for the erection of these elevators. In the next place, each one of these elevatora is to be equipped with all necessary treating and cleaning apparatus, so that for dis-

eased or disabled grain, so to speak, in any season and more especially in seasons such as we had two years ago when there was a great quantity of that kind of grain through the Northwest, we shall have at these terminal elevators proper and adequate machinery for cleaning the grain as to drying, or any other way in which it is treated. That will be a very important office that the internal storage elevators will perform. The site of each elevator will have to be made a terminal point, and the grain stored there will break its passage. In so far as the rates of transport are concerned, these are matters which come under the general transport system; and the rates will be according to the railroad schedules over which the railway commission will have, at it has now, ultimate jurisdiction, if there is dissatisfaction with reference to the rates. Warehouse receipts will be given for the grain when stored in these terminal elevators just as they are granted at Fort William, and there will be & registration system for the receipts and cancellations when the grain is shipped out.
Grain will be inspected also for mills in the vicinity of these storage centres. We have already under the Act power to appoint an inspector for a milling concern, inspectors' fees to be paid, any deficiency to be made up by the mill itself. We inserted that provision in the Act some two years ago. If grain exchanges are established at the places where these terminal elevators are, then provisions will be made for the inspection of grain consigned to members of the exchange so as to facilitate their operations. Otherwise and beyond these matters, I do not see that any interference will be had with the general work of inspection of outward bound grain via Winnipeg and the lakes.

The usefulness of these
terminal elevators will depend partly upon the facilities that they offer, partly upon the charges for the use of such facilities and partly upon the railroad carriage. How far can the minister inform the House as to the arrangement regarding road carriage?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
So far as the charges
to be imposed and the facilities to be given by the railways are concerned, these matters have not yet been taken up by the commission. These elevators will not be ready for the receipt of grain until probably December of this year or January of next year; and in the meantime the Board of Grain Commissioners will have to take up the whole question as to the modus opex-

andi and the charges, so Jar as they rest in the hands of the board itself, which will be the charges for storage, cleaning and everything like that. 'So far as the railway rates are concerned, that matter will remain, as I have said, in the hands of the transport authorities, and the Board of Grain Commissioners will take the matter np with them. I suppose what my hon. friend has in mind is what may come to be a backhaul >at certain times, namely, grain in the vicinity going into the storage elevators, then when going out again having to traverse part of the ground which it has previously traversed to get in. There is an arrangement which the railway companies make in the United States for this class of elevators; and I presume the same arrangement will be made with our own railways, both as regards the back-haul for the grain alone and as regards the freight rates charged for what we call milling in transit. These matters have not as yet been taken up by the Board, although they are being considered; but they will be taken up in the summer and provided for by the time the elevators are ready to receive grain.

The point that I want to
get at and that I cannot imagine has been left in doubt at all np to the present time is as to whether there will be a storage-intransit rate on the grain, or a local rate for part of the haul. If there is to be a storage-in-transit Tate on an absolute equality with the rate without storage, that will make for the usefulness of the storage facilities offered. If, however, there is not an arrangement for a storagedn-transit rate which shall be on an equality with the present rate without storage, then the usefulness of the storage facilities provided will be very much minimized; and I assume that that is not a question in doubt at the present time, but that the Government and the minister know absolutely whether a storage-in-transit rate on an absolute equality with the present rate without storage will be given or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: So far as that is concerned, whilst I think there is no doubt at all that there will be storage-in-transit rates, these have not yet been fixed, and they will not be fixed until the Board of Grain Commissioners take the matter up with the railway authorities first and then with the Board of Railway Commissioners.

This is a rather serious matter. The Government has entered upon this policy, presumably for the benefit of the producers and through them of the country generally; and on the authority of the minister, the Government does not know to-day whether that policy is going to be efficient, not knowing what the railroad rates are to be. I can hardly imagine a Government undertaking this policy in that condition. Surely it was quite possible to know a year ago whether there was to be a storage-in-transit rate on an equality with the rate without storage or not. It was not necessary to wait until the storage was provided before the rates could be arrived at. I have hopes that the condition is better than the hon. minister has seen fit to lay it before the House; but if it is as he has actually laid it before the House, it certainly is not a fortunate condition.

Has the minister considered the question that came up when the original Bill was before the House last year in regard to elevators for treating diseased and disabled grain? I refer to the noxious weeds that are cleaned out of the grain at these elevators. It seems a remarkable state of affairs that we should have elevators for treating diseased grain, and yet that part of the material handled which offers the greatest menace to the country is scattered broadcast. I feel that I am well within the mark when I say that the spread of noxious weeds throughout Canada is costing this country, I will not say how many millions, but certainly high up in the millions every year, and presents a serious problem in every province in Canada. So I do not think this Bill will be complete until the Government sees to it that none of the noxious weefd seeds that are cleaned out of the grain in these elevators are allowed to be scattered broadcast throughout the country. I think this matter should have engaged the attention of the Government, and I hope it will engage their attention in the near future. I know that the provincial legislatures have the power to enact laws to control this matter, but I believe it would be more effective and more satisfactory if this Government were to take it in hand. What would you think of a hospital which treated people for contagious disease yet made no effort to prevent the spread of that disease? Yet we have a similar condition here, but instead of preventing the spread of its disease it is encouraged. This spread of

noxious weeds I consider a most serious menace to the farmers of Canada at the present time. We speak of the high cost of living in this country. Why, there would be a living for one-third of the people of Canada in saving the losses that take place every year through the spreading of this terrible pest of noxious weeds throughout the country.
I desire to ask the minister a question which I put on a former occasion-with regard to the architects of these buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is going off on another branch of the subject, I should like to have opportunity first to answer my hon. friend from South Oxforfd (Mr. Sutherland).
I was not going to deal with the question of the screenings.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As to the question of
noxious weeds in the screenings, I may say that for the past year that has engaged, and is now engaging, the earnest attention of the Grain Board. We have added the machinery of the chemical labatory, and we have at present two men, thoroughly equipped in their several departments, who are paying particular attention to that branch of the subject. They are working together with the officers of the Grain Board and are doing all that possibly can be done at the present time to get at a basis of facts with reference to noxious weeds in the several grades of grain, and also with reference to the values of these different seeds, mostly weed seeds, and the useful purposes to which they may be put. On that basis of fact, when it is made, there can be built up a system of taking care of these leavings of the good grain and making those leavings of economical use, for it is quite possible to make these screenings useful as feed for stock of various kinds. Of course my hon. friend is entirely right, that noxious weeds are a great detriment to the country. The ' farmer's pest ' is always with most of the farmers of the country. And, whilst we would like to see the time approach when there will be no weeds on any farm in Canada, yet, the millennium so far as that is concerned, is a good way in the distance. But that does not justify the relaxation of any effort towards restricting, diminishing and if possible eradicating this pest. The provincial governments have their parts to do in the matter, and they are moving in that direction; the Department of Agriculture of the Dominion and

the departments of agriculture of the several provinces co-operate in this work. Whatever can be done by the Grain Board, and-after they have mapped out their work in this matter, whatever can be done by Dominion legislation to diminish this pest, will be done. And I hope to be able, at the next session of Parliament, to give a fairly clear idea as to what we think can be done by the Grain Board and through Parliament in this direction.

The weed problem is a very important problem in the West and has been so for many years. Some of the weeds we have are so tenacious that it is almost impossible to cultivate them out of the ground. But I must say that the theories of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) with regard to the desirability of having weedless farms and how to get rid of weeds will not, I fear, carry much weight in the West. For I may tell my hon. friend that the farmers of the West take very little stock in his advice about how to farm. In fact, it is one of the jokes among our people that the hon. gentleman's remedy for the evils that afflict us is mixed farming. I suppose that panacea would cover weed evils also, according to the hon. gentleman. Perhaps he will correct me if I am wrong. Evidently, he has not given that problem the mature thought that he has given to the other questions on which he has laid down his doctrine. At any rate, it is a joke among our farming community, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with all his college degrees, and even with his high standing as an orator, has one way of -settling all our difficulties and that is by advising us to go into mixed farming. It is something like adequate protection-there is supposed to be something in it for everybody. But I can tell the hon. gentleman how he could have done more to keep down the weeds than in any other way, and that is by allowing us to grow such short-maturing crops as barley. There was nothing for which the open market that at one time seemed to be -so near to us was more prized by our farmers than for this very reason, that it would have given them an opportunity to clear their farms of weeds. The worst weed we have, perhaps, is wild oats. There is so much oil in the seed that even though you summer-fallow your ground for four or five years, yet the seed will not rot. It is only by some system of growing crops that will mature before the wild oats that you can compel this weed to grow itsqlf out. As I -say, there was nothing for which

the open market was more desired than to enable the farmers to clear their farms by cultivating these quickly-maturing crops.

Eeciprocity would send
more rain, too, would it not?

I do not know whether or not it would have sent more rain, but it would have produced better conditions than those that exist under this Government. The people of Canada had the opportunity of Choosing between a progressive, statesmanlike policy and a reactionary policy; they took the latter and we see the results. We saw the results before 1896 and we have seen them since 1911. If the people of Canada had accepted the progressive policy, I believe that there would be no such financial depression in Canada as there is today. Why is it that in England they never were so prosperous as they are now? Why is it that the city of Toronto is more prosperous than it has been? You can scarcely rent a house in the city of Toronto to-day because the policy of this Government makes Toronto prosperous and makes our farming communities not prosperous.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Now suppose we
get back to the Bill.

The hon. member for
South Oxford might have been told to stay with the Bill and the hon. member for South Grey as well. I am afraid that the advice of the hon. minister on the weed question or anything else that pertains to farming, will not carry very much weight. As a farming instructor, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce is a joke. When the western farmer asks for anything he is told -tq go into mixed farming; that advice is pretty well played out. We must get what is coming to us, not periodical lectures on mixed farming by a gentleman who does not know anything about farming. When the minister had his Bill before the House on a previous occasion he was in a hurry to get it through at six o'clock and he promised to give us some figures with regard to the relationship between the architect and the contractor in connection with these elevators. He informed us that the architect was a Nova Scotian, although he belonged he thought, to the firm that was constructing the elevator. Would he kindly give us such information as he can with regard to that dual capacity?

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat stated that the remarks which I made were outside the scope of the measure now before the committee. I think I was well within the mark, because the provisions of the Bill deal with exactly those things to which I was referring. When the hon. member refers to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce as a joke in western Canada when he undertakes to enact legislation in their interest-
I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to misrepresent me. I did not say that; I said that when he turned farming instructor we regarded that as a joke.

Permit me to say that when the hon. gentleman endeavours to make the people of this House believe that by growing barley he can get ahea'd of the wild oats, he is a joke himself. I say that you will have difficulty in beating out the wild oats by growing barley or any other kind of grain, for the oats will germinate just as readily and mature just as quickly as the barley. Even if cut before maturity, the grain will germinate and grow, and the roots will grow as well. This talk about the western farmer being handicapped by the people of Canada because they have refused him reciprocity is getting a little stale in this House. This House is being asked, day after day, week after week, and session after session, to pass legislation in the interests of the people of Canada anfd particularly in the interests of the people of the West. We are building the Hudson Bay railway, and we are building storage elevators, and the people of the West want cars right at their doors so that they will not have to build granaries. If the people of the older provinces were to ask for favours of this kind, they would be laughed at. We find no fault with the granting of facilities to the people of the West, but I think the hon. gentleman goes to extremes when he criticises the minister, who is doing everything in his power to look after the interests of the people of western Canada.

I was surprised to hear the negative and noncommittal statement of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce this morning with reference to a question brought to his attention by the hon. member for Edmonton. A couple of years ago this House undertook to pass the Canada Grain Act, which we are now asked to amend by this Bill. As I understand it, the object of the Canada Grain Act was to regulate and correct certain conditions and

abuses that surrounded the marketing of the farmers' grain, particularly in western Canada. Under this Act the Board of Grain Commissioners was appointed by this Government, and are carrying on the work of making regulations in respect of the storage, handling and marketing of grain. We have been watching very closely the operations of this Board of Grain Commissioners, and, so far as I can discover, the only radical change that they have accomplished is that in certain instances they have increased the fees chargeable against the farmers' grain for handling at the terminal elevators. This Government have inaugurated a new policy; they have undertaken to establish interior terminal elevators at various points through the West. The only possible good that could come from the establishment of these interior elevators would be to relieve the conditions of congestion that have prevailed year after year because of the inability of the railroad companies to handle the farmers' grain in the marketing season, and, in some cases, the inability of the terminals at Fort William and Port Arthur to receive the grain when it is brought there by the transport companies. In my judgment the very first thing, the Government, embarking on this policy, should have considered, is the question of keeping down the cost of storage and of transportation. If the effect of this policy is going to be that, in addition to the necessary extra charges for handling, that is unloading, storing and reloading of the grain at these interior terminal elevators, the grain grower will also have to pay two local rates on his wheat, to these interior elevators and from there to the final terminals, if we may use that term, at Fort William and Port Arthur, then I think that experience will prove and prove very shortly that this whole policy of interior terminal elevators will fall to the ground. In my judgment the very first duty of the minister responsible for the inauguration of this policy was to have made arrangements with the transportation companies as to the rates that would be charged for grain shipped to these interior elevators, and from them to the final terminals at Fort William and Port Arthur. The charges for handling grain at these terminals are inevitable. But if to these charges, as the minister will see, there is to be added an extra charge owing to the payment of local instead of through freight rates, the grain growers of the West will be very loath indeed to ship their grain to these interior storage elevators. The minister has absolutely failed to carry into effect the neces-fMr. Neely.]
sary measures to make these interior terminal elevators in the country a success. He now tells us that the question of rates is all in the hands of the Railway Commission. We quite appreciate that and we know that, year after year, these matters of freight rates in the West have been before the commission. In a case inaugurated something over two years ago a decision was handed down recently. Full two years had been spent on this question of rates. There is no doubt that if the farmers object to paying two local rates, and this matter is to be brought to the attention of the Board of Railway Commissioners, there will be an interminable delay before the matter can be remedied, if indeed it is ever remedied in that manner. Surely the minister does not propose to tell us that he jumped into this thing in the dark, when he decided on the policy of erecting a considerable number of more or less expensive interior storage elevators throughout the West, without working out to its final conclusion the bene. ficial effects that that policy might or might not bring to the grain growers. I say that is surely a serious admission on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if he proposes to make it, as apparently he has made it this morning. If the minister had found it impossible to make an arrangement with the transportation companies for the continuance of a through rate 12 noon, in connection with these interior storage elevators, a knowledge of that fact would have had a very important bearing on the decision of this House to agree to the policy of establishing these interior storage elevators. The minister knows that if the cost of using them is too large the farmers will shirk using them. From the answers to questions I have asked the. minister, I do not think that the Government so far has got along very far in the actual construction of these elevators and I trust that before . the minister goes any further with their erection or incurs any further expenditure, he will ascertain if it is not possible to have the railroad companies agree to give a through rate to Fort William, Vaucouver, Hudson bay or other final terminal points; because I am quite satisfied that if some such arrangement is not made the beneficial result of the building of these interior storage elevators will be nullified to a large extent, if not entirely. So far the passing of the Canada Grain Act a couple of years ago has resulted only in the increase of the cost of handling and marketing grain. The minister knows that

the great cause of loss of profit to the farmer is the cost of production of his grain in the West. That cost has markedly increased owing to various things, not altogether the increased cost of handling, other contributing causes are the increased cost of lake shipment, of ocean shipment and of labour. The minister has read the report of the commission appointed by the Saskatchewan Government over a year ago to investigate the grain trade in which they point out that notwithstanding that last year's crop was the best the West has ever produced, both as to quality and quantity, the margin of profit was .less last year than for many years previously. The commission pointed out that from 1909 to 1913 the cost of production of grain in western Canada had increased from twelve and one-half per cent to fifteen per cent, and one of the items in this increase has 'been the increase in the cost of storage, handling and marketing. The crux of the success of this elevator scheme depends upon keeping the cost of the use of these elevators down to a minimum; and if the farmer, say at Swift Current, who uses the terminal interior storage elevator at Moosejaw, has to pay a local rate from Swift Current to Moosejaw and another local rate to Fort William, or even if he has to pay one local rate with his through rate from Moosejaw to Fort William, the result will be that the grain grower will find it quite impossible to use these means of protection in times of congestion. I have been trying to get, by questions and returns, certain facts in connection with the operations of the Board of Grain Commissioners at Fort William and Port Arthur. I want to draw the minister's attention to a return dated March 2, of this year -which I moved for and which called for	'
The quantities of wheat, by grade, received into the terminal elevators at Port William and Port Arthur from the date of the weigh-up in 1910, to the date of weigh-up in 1911, the same for 1911-1912, and the same for 1912-1913.
I have gone over these returns and I find a very remarkable omission in all of them. My idea in moving for the return was to find out whether or not the terminal elevators were giving any better results under the control of the Board of Grain Commissioners than formerly. I am absolutely unable to come to any conclusion in that respect. These elevators show a certain amount of shortage or overage each year. The reason why the returns are unsatisfactory is that there is no balance carried forward from year to year in the case of each elevator. The bank account is apparently absolutely closed at the end of each year, or at each annual weigh-up, and the elevator starts out with a clean sheet for each succeeding year. The amounts are given for each year, the shipments in and the shipments out and the weigh-up, but there is no balance carried forward from year to year. There seems to be a remarkable omission in the returns and it prevents me from arriving at the information I had in my mind when I moved for them. There is no balance carried forward from the weigh-up of the year 1911 to the year 19111912. I would like to ask the minister if he does not think that he would be well advised to take into his consideration the question brought to our attention by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), and to see, before there is any further prosecution of this policy of building interior elevators, if there is any possibility of coming to a definite arrangement in regard to the matter. That could be done quickly, but the minister has not taken any steps even to ascertain whether it can or can not be done. As far as I could gather from his remarks, he never made an attempt to make such a specific arrangement. I think it is important that the attempt should be made now before the policy is prosecuted further. Surely the minister does not want to load up the country with a large capital expenditure for the building and maintenance of these elevators if the elevators are not going to pay, and if, to make them pay he has to compel the farmer to pay a great deal more in charges than he can afford.
Is the minister not going to answer any of the questions that were asked him?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I did not quite oatoh my hon. friend's question.

The minister will remember that, during the consideration of some amendments to the Grain Act, or perhaps it was while his Estimates were under discussion, I asked him as to the circumstances under which gravel had been procured for the construction of the elevator at Moosejaw, and I asked him also how the different railways were to get in. The minister said that he would have a letter written to the engineer and see if he could make any report upon it. I asked him in regard to the access of the different railways and he said I could see the plans if I went to the department. I went to the department but found that they were gone.

I also spoke of the combined position of architect and contractor and pointed out that the other contractors were at a disadvantage because the successful contractor was associated with the architect. None of these points were discussed at length, but the minister stated that we could discuss them later on; he was very anxious to get the item we were considering through before six o'clock. I see that he has not anticipated the repetition of these questions and I do not know whether we will have another chance of having them answered during the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
What I said at
the time-we were discussing Estimates -was that I would reserve one item in the Steamship Subsidies Estimates and that when we came to take them up afterwards I would be prepared to answer any question in regard to elevators and elevator construction. My hon. friend will remember that.

Yes, I was in error
when I said it was the Grain Act that we were considering.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
When we were putting
through the resolution upon which the Bill is founded, the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) asked if I would answer some of these questions at the time the Bill was being put through. I said that I would, and the hon. gentleman himself also put some queries that he would like to have answered. Therefore, I have been looking towards the discussion of these matters when we came to the single item that had been left in the Estimates. However, in face of the remarks which have been made by my hon. friends opposite, I will try to answer the questions now. Some of them I am going to allude to because they are important, and others I am not going to allude to because they refer to a little joking in reference to myself, and that is not important enough to take up the time of this committee with. I have never posed as a farm instructor, and all I did do was to exercise my individual right as an humble observer, and in looking over the situation in the West I conceived an opinion that in some way or other mixed farming might be more extensively prosecuted than it hitherto has been. I had the temerity to utter that opinion in the House on several occasions. I am quite sure that nobody has been hurt because I did utter it, and 1 am also quite sure that I have not lost the respect of any good, well-grounded

farmer in the West because I mentioned that opinion. I defer entirely in connection with all that kind of knowledge to my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles). He is a past master in all those questions of wild oats and oil seed out in all the different ranges where weeds grow and flourish and pester the farmer of the West. He lives in that country and ought to know a great deal more about these things than I do.
As to gravel, which has greatly disturbed my hon. friend, I am afraid I will have to ask him to excuse me from going deeply into the gravel question, because I do not think it is important. We make a contract with a contractor. We pay him for his construction, and cement is used in that construction. The contractor has to look for his own materials and he gets them where ' he best can and at the best price he can for himself. We are not concerned as to where he buys his cement, except that we would like him to get it, and he practically does get it, in 'Canada. We are not concerned as to where he gets his gravel. We are concerned with two things, and with two things only. These are that the cement shall be the proper thing and that the gravel shall be the proper kind, and that the two shall make the construction according to the ideas of the supervising officer who is our own engineer. As to any troubles which have arisen in the path of the contractor towards his finding the gravel and getting it to the place of construction, I do not think that is anything of interest to this House.
I have no information upon it. All that I require my engineer to do is to supervise the construction of the work and see that the gravel and cement are proper. That he does, and that he reports to me. So much with reference to the gravel business. The next is as to the nearness of contact between the contractor and the engineer. Plans are prepared by different individuals and architects for the building of an elevator. These plans are gone over very carefully by our own architect and engineer. The plans he considers the best for that particular elevator are recommended by him and they are accepted on his recommendation by the board. Then it is the duty of the supervising engineer, who has no affiliation with the contractor in any way, to see that the building is constructed upon these plans and specifications, and that he does. There is no collusion and could not possibly be any collusion be-

tween the architect and the contractor in that respect. The architect's plans are there; if they are not good they are not taken, if they are good they are taken, and when they are taken the plans and specifications have to be lived up to according to the direction of our own engineer in charge, and in whom I have full faith. Mr. Howe is one of the most capable young men in his profession in Canada, and he is also as straight-forward and as honest as a man can be. I have every confidence, as has the Board of Grain Commissioners, that he does his work well and sees that the contractor does his work well also.
With reference to my hon. friend (Mr. Neely), who made the general assertion that after all these three or four years of effort under the Canada Grain Act, the only benefit that has come to the West was that they had had their fees and charges Taised, which, however, is not the fact. I may say that the enunciation of a statement like that is all the argument I want to use against my hon. friend's fairly long criticism of the Grain Commission and of the working of the Grain Act. I put that to the farmers of the West, to the shippers of the West, and to the grain growers of the West. Here on one side is a statement made by a member of this House that all the good that has come to the West out of the whole Grain Act and out of its administration under the commission is that they have had their fees made higher.
1 said all I had been able to discover.

My hon. -friend will not
depreciate himself so much as to say to this House that there is- anything discoverable that he has not been able to discover. He has not so placed himself generally before this House as being a man who feels that he is lacking in knowledge in any way; the opposite is rather the case. He is an authority upon western matters and I have never questioned his authority, and it will not do for -him to try to escape the mild criticism I am giving him by entering the plea he has just put in. I will let -his statement go to the farmers, to the shippers, and to the grain men of the West and he will not find a baker's dozen of them who have had anything to do with -and any experience under the Canada Grain Act, who will stand by him in that assertion. He has quoted the commission appointed by the Government of Saskatchewan, by which he sets great store, and I read the report of 226
that commission -and I ta-pprove very largely of that report. I hope I will not raise the ire of my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Know-les) when I venture to express the opinion that after having read that re-port I think i-t is a very excellent report, and my hon. friend oan take that report from the first page to the last and he will find -almost unceasing commendation of the work of the Grain Commission and of the Canada Grain Act.
Where is the commendation that my hon. friend speaks of?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If th-e hon. gentleman has read the report he will find it on almost every page.
What is the date of that report?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I cannot be expected to
keep such dates in my head, but m.y hon. friend comes from Saskatchewan and surely he knows the date of the report of his own provincial government and he is not asking me for information in that respect.
I wanted to get it down on ' Hansard.'

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
These are apparently questions which flow out fatuously from the hon. gentleman and are not meant for any practical result. With reference -to the storage elevators, my hon. friend who last criticised them, gave the impression to the House that in the first place the only reason why these elevators were -constructed was to enable people to store grain on its way to the ultimate market. That is one reason, but that is not the only reason. Even suppose we let him rest on his own argument, that the man who puts his grain into the storage elevator will have to pay -the local rate- from the Iplace he takes it to the storage elevator, and then when the storage has served its purpose that the local rate will have to be paid again when it is sent to its ultimate market, are there not -still other advantages to come from the erection of storage elevators in the West? I think the hon. member will not say that the only advantage is a resting place for -a little while -for grain on its way towards its ultimate market. The storage elevator is also to enable men who wish to take advantage of the market, -and are able to take advantage of the market, and who have no grain houses and storage places of their jwn, -to put their grain into these storage houses nearby their own farms, to get their warehouse receipt, to finance themselves



upon that receipt, and if they wish, to hold the grain in an independent position for a future market. They have had no conveniences for that upon their own farms, and I hope my hon. friend from Moosejaw will not think I am unduly criticising the western farmers because they have not these conveniences, but the fact is that as a rule they do not have them. Here we have machinery placed by this Parliament or by the Government in which they may store the grain and hold it there, financing themselves to the extent that the warehouse receipt gives them the capacity for so doing, and avoiding the necessity of throwing their grain in with the general rush, when the price is apt to go down, as it did last year, and holding it themselves for a future market. I think that is a great advantage, especially if what happened two years ago should repeat itself. If you have any season during which we raise in the West two hundred or two hundred and fifty million bushels of wheat, when, owing to the season, a large proportion of that goes bad an*d needs to be treated, these internal storage elevators equipped thoroughly for drying and for treating grain will save so much to the aggregate farming interests of the West that they will pay for themselves one hundred times over. I think every one will admit that. In a season such as we had two years ago, with an aggregate output of two hundred and fifty million bushels in the West, elevators at Calgary, at Saskatoon, and at Moosejaw, ready for storage to the extent they will be, with treating machinery in full equipment, they will be an insurance and a benefit to the farmers of the West which it is very difficult to estimate in money value. These are advantages that ought not to be lost track of in connection with the other.
As to the matter of rates, we are not legis-, lating in this Canada Grain Act for rates on railways. Rates on railways are fixed in different Acts and by a different authority from the Grain Commission. I am quite willing -I am rather glad in fact-that my hon. friend's criticisms have gone upon the paper. They will be embalmed in the treasure house of this Parliament-the inevitable and inexhaustible * Hansard.' There they will be; and we shall compare notes next year when we come together again, when the capacities of ' Hansard ' will be just as large as they are to-day, and we shall see how we make out in the way of these comparisons. I have no fears as regards that. The Grain Commission 
and my department have already considered this matter to a certain extent and will further consider it; and when the time comes for the movement of the grain and the operation of these internal storehouses, I have no doubt that a satisfactory arrangement will be reached.
I do not know that there are any other questions that I have missed answering. I want to answer every question; and if I incorporate into my answers a little mild criticism now and again of my two hon. friends who are facing me, it is just to show that I am generous enough to give back a little of what they so generously gave to me.

It is very remarkable that the hon. minister, with all that fund of information which he has, which he should have and which he is expected, as the head of his department to have at his command, in speaking of the improvements in the handling and the marketing of the grain of the West, that have been brought about under his administration, after all has had to fall back for his verification on a report published by a commission appointed by the Government of the province of Saskatchewan. Whilst he has challenged my statement, he has not given, so far as I can learn, any concrete evidence that he has concrete illustrations in his own mind as to what improvements have been brought about; but he simply makes the general statement, basing it on the report which I have just mentioned, that such is the case. I am willing to take the minister's word for it, but I would have preferred if he had given us some concrete illustrations as to the improvements brought about since he has been in charge of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and consequently of shipping conditions in the West.
The minister tells us that, when this policy gets on a little further and when there are eight or ten of these elevators in operation, this question of the rates will be worked out satisfactorily. That information is very satisfactory, but it is very indefinite. The minister does not at all meet the point which I am trying to make, namely, that, before launching on this policy of building a large number of storage elevators throughout the West, at a greater or less expense, he and his department have made no definite arrangements. I use for illustration only this one particular benefit that the farmers expect to derive from these storage elevators, that .is, a place of storage in time of congestion.

I quite agree with the minister that they may be of great benefit in other directions; but the point I am making is that, if the financial benefit that may be derived by the farmers from the erection of these elevators is to he handed over to the railway companies by the paying of extra rates for transport, then the whole .scheme falls to the ground. That is my contention, as the minister knows; but he has managed, in that very able manner of his, to evade it entirely in his reply. The minister is very capable when it comes to making a general statement; hut when it comes to giving particulars, I am afraid I have to admit that, apart from the criticism of my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), that he is not an authority on farming, he is not just as great an authority as he should 'be on matters intimately connected with his department.
On April 22 I asked the minister a few -questions, which h-e was good enough to answer, with reference to what the Board of Grain Commissioners had done regarding the establishment of sample markets in western -Canada. Here is a little bit of inside history given in answer to my questions. The questions and answers are as follows:
Mr. Neely:
1.	Has the Board of Grain Commissioners recommended to the Government the establishment of sample markets in western Canada?
2.	If so, what date did they recommend for the establishment of sample markets and at what points?
3.	Has the Government passed any Order in Council respecting the matter, as required by the Grain Act?
4.	If so, what dates were fixed and what points were selected for the establishment of these sample markets?
5.	If such Order in Council was passed, has it been given effect? If not, why not?
Mr. George E. Foster:
1.	Yes.
2.	September, 1913. The board afterwards-*
I Mo not know what ' afterwards ' means-
-changed the date of their recommendation to December 15,	1913; Winnipeg and Fort
William.
3.	Yes.
4.	December 15, 1913, but subsequently indefinitely postponed; Winnipeg and Fort William.
5.	No. The crop of 1913 was of unusually high quality and remarkably uniform. It was harvested early and placed rapidly upon the market. By the date set, most of the wheat had passed out of first hands, and the farmers therefore would have got little if any advantage from putting the sample market into operation.
226i
If the first date recommended, namely, September 1, 1913, had been adopted, and the Order in Council passed in accordance therewith, this -answer would not have been on the Order Paper as to the crop having passed out of the farmers' hands previous to the establishment of the sample market. I am giving this as an illustration to show what I think everybody in the grain trade in the West knows perfectly well, that, through inexperience or something of the sort, a certain policy entered into last year for the hanMling of last year's crop was recommended by the Board of Grain Commissioners, an Order in Council was passed based upon that recommendation, and what happened? When it came to the working out of the policy, certain insuperable difficulties faced both the members of the board and the minister, with the result that that Order in Council was not carried into effect, but was indefinitely postponed. The recommendations of the Board of Grain Com-. missioners and the operations of the minister and department during this year will show whether or not they propose to take up for the coming year the proposals which they made last year, but which they dropped. I am just using that as an illustration to show how a policy may be adopted without due consideration, and that those who have adopted the policy may find themselves up against insurmountable difficulties, with the result that the policy has to be dropped. I would not like to see that occur in the case of the interior storage elevators, because I agree with the minister that great benefits may result therefrom. That is, benefits will result if the railway companies are not permitted to rob the farmers of those benefits by charging them double rates instead of single through rates to the head terminals at Fort William and other points.
Can the minister tell what will be the storage rates in these elevators?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
These have not been fixed yet by the Grain Commission. I may remind my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) that he is in error when he says that the only thing that had happened as the result of the Grain Act and its administration under the Grain Commission was an increase in the rates. I do not follow him in that, for the rates for storage in elevators are exactly the same as they were last yeaT, under the amended Act they remained the same as under the former

Act; there has been no raising of rates in any respect.
What about the license and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I did not imagine that my hon. friend was so interested in looking after the interests of the elevators, these big corporations, that we would raise this row because they were made to pay a fair license fee. That fee does not come from the farmer, and I think that the elevators are quite able to pay it; and so long as I have the administration of the Grain Act I propose that they shall pay something for the privileges that they enjoy. But so far as the fees charged the farmers are concerned, whether in the country elevators, the elevators in the West or the terminal elevators the farmers pay not one single tenth of a cent more than they paid before.
My hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) asks what will be the storage rates. I have already answered that the storage rates have not been settled. They will certainly not be greater than the rates at present in force in Fort William. Whether they shall be less or not will depend upon the opinion of the Grain Commission. I may say that while, as minister, I am responsible in the end, yet I have thrown absolutely their full share of the responsibility for these matters upon the Grain Commission. They are three men whom I believe to be good men and capable. They are in the business and all the time they are going, up and down the whole line of transport and amongst the people who are engaged in this business. I think they have the best opportunity of examination and of reaching conclusions, and I stand by the Grain Commission. I do not think there is a single thing yet in which I have been at cross purposes with them. I think they know better what ought to be carried out than I do. At the same time, I do not abdicate my position as being responsible and there is very little that the Grain Commission does that I do not discuss with them in one form or another.

The statement from the minister that the storage rates will not be greater than the rates at Fort William will not afford much encouragement to the grain grower or grain handler of the West. The storage rates at Fort William have been one of the grievances in the trade. For instance, they charge for winter storage one cent per month, whereas, if the grain Were on this side of the lakes it would be carried at one and one-half cent for the winter season.

If the internal elevators are to be of any considerable value for storage in the West, rates will have to be considerably reduced as compared with those at Fort William. Now, I agree largely with what the minister has said as to the value of these internal elevators in the West. One advantage will be that the crop can be handled more quickly than would be possible if the trains had to go down to Fort William and back. Another advantage will be that if these elevators are equipped with proper cleaning machinery, the grain can be cleaned	in	these elevatorsand	the	owner of the grain will
not have to pay freight on weeds and seeds that are of very small commercial value and that are not wanted in the East. I am not sure that it is good policy to give out the ideas concerning the western country that freight rates are going to be quite as bad as represented by my hon. friend from Humboldt. I noticed that the hon. minister was not in a position to correct that. I do not know where my hon. friend from Humbo'ldt gathered the idea he gave to the House. For instance, he gave a concrete case where they will have to pay a local freight from Swift Current to Moose-jaw and another from Moosejaw to Fort William. I think he has been misinformed in that.

I did not say anyUiing
about what they had to pay; I asked if the minister had made any arrangement.

I gathered that the minister was going to take credit later on for fixing these rates. As a matter of fact, the rates had been in force for many years, and I suppose that these internal elevators will enjoy the same privileges as the millers in their elevators. Grain will be shipped on through rates to Fort William and will pay a stop-over of two cents per 100 pounds for cleaning. I think that is a reasonable charge and the farmers could hardly expect better. These are the rates going East; the rates going West are somewhat different, and they, perhaps, will have to be corrected.
How long is the stopover?
I think the millers are allowed six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As to the point men-toned by my hon. friend, the feeling that the rates for storage at the terminal elevators at Fort William have been too high, we really are not in a position to under-

stand the inside workings o'f the elevator system under the established rates until we have had the experience of a full year of an elevator owned and operated by the Dominion. The Grain Commissioners, of course, are watching that matter very closely, as also is my department. At the end of the year we shall have means of estimating what are fair and reasonable charges for storage at the terminal elevators. I am not making any pronouncement at the present time. But the Grain Commissioners' report, when it comes down, will, I think, give an intimation of the views that the Grain Commission has formed in that regard. And, I may say-putting it negatively-those views are not of a tendency to increase the cost and charges at the terminal elevators. The whole matter, as my hon. friend will see, assumes an entirely different aspect as the basis for judgment concerning proper charges, when the operation of the Government elevator has proceeded for the space of one year.
What are the winter storage charges at the Midland elevator ?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have not the information before me just at the present time.
One cent and a half a bushel.
What is the storage charge at the Port Colborne elevator ?
One cent and a half is the maximum rate; if the grain is taken out within the winter period the rate is one-thirtieth of a cent a day.

The Port Colborne elevator is the property of the Dominion Government. It was built by the Dominion Government at the cost of the Dominion; it has been in operation for a considerable number of years, and there ought to be adequate knowledge in the department by this time as to whether the charge at the Port Colborne elevator, which is on all-fours with the private elevators at Midland, is or is not below a reasonable figure. It is hard to make anybody understand that Government money employed at Port Colborne in the erection of an elevator should have less earning power than Government money employed in the construction of an elevator at Fort William. I think the minister has been rather slow, if I may say so, in making up his mind as to what the storage charges should be, especially when he is establishing a new policy, carrying out a new principle and making a very large expenditure of money. Without wishing to delay the committee, I take this
opportunity of emphasizing to the minister the views of the hon. member for Humboldt that the value of the interior elevators depends upon the charges made foT their use, both in respect of storage and of transportation to and from them. I am not pleased to hear the minister explain at such length and with such emphasis the additional benefits that will be conferred by reason of the elevators offering more than simple storage. It seems to me as if he were discounting a possibility of higher charges for the additional advantages that we all hope will come from the construction of these elevators. I have said before, and I am going to take the liberty of saying again, that in the face of a falling world's market of wheat; in the face of increase of production in new and competitive countries, if we are going to stay in the wheat business, we must cut our costs to the bone. This is not a matter concerning only the farmer of the West; it is a matter concerning everybody in Canada whose business is dependent directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, upon the success and expansion of wheat growing on the western prairies. If it is possible for the minister to cut the cost of storage; if it is possible for him to cut the expense connected with these interior storage elevators, it is his duty to do so, ini the interests not merely of the farmers but of the Dominion of Canada as [DOT]a whole, in order that there may be a further expansion of the wheat-growing industry on the prairies and in order that the wheat growers of the West may he able to compete in the markets of the world under the adverse conditions which are increasing from season to season. I say it is his business to cut those costs laibsolutely to the bone, and it is not going to meet the case to say that such and such charges prevail some place else; that there axe going to be special advantages in the use of these elevators and that the farmers ought, therefore, to pay ian extra special charge. If the purpose of the Government in making these expenditures and in providing these facilities is to be reached, there must be a cut of costs absolutely to the minimum.
In connection with the cost of use of these elevators, let me refer to the back-haul to whioh the minister himself has alluded. The elevators at Saskatoon and at Moose-jaw are situated about midway in the province of Saskatchewan from east to west. Very much more wheat is raised in Saskatchewan east of Moosejaw and east of Saska-

toon than west of Moosejaw and west of Saskatoon, therefore if the elevators at Saskatoon and Moosejaw aire to be used by the Wheat growers living to the east of them an additional haul to market-the backhaul of which the minister spoke-is involved. I am not dictating as to what can or what should be done, but it is perfectly clear that in respect of the wheat of eastern Saskatchewan, which has to pay a backhaul to get the benefit of these elevators, unless there is some special advantage in connection with the freight rates, these elevators are going to be of very little use to that part of the province of Saskatchewan which raises the largest proportion of the wheat of the province. This special advantage would mean a cut below the ordinary rate in respect of the wheat taking this back-haul. I do not know whether or not that is possible; I am not going to discuss that point. I merely point out that unless something of that kind is done, considerably more than half the wheat grown in the province of Saskatchewan cannot get the benefit of those elevator facilities at Saskatoon or Moosejaw excepting at a prohibitive cost.
I am sorry that the minister is not able to give us the charges that he proposes to impose for the use of these elevators. The hon. member for Huntingdon has said that there is a milling-in-transit rate on the railroads which would be available to the elevators. That is quite possible. I know that there is a milling-in-transit rate, but I also know that special charges might be be levied on grain for storage which is not levied in the case of grain for milling. There is always the posibility of an advance to the disadvantage of a new institution. I wish to emphasize the necessity, in the interests of the Government, in the interests of the reputation of the Dominion, in the interests of the country at large, and in the interests of the farmers, that this matter of cost should have the fullest attention of the minister and that the cost should be cut absolutely to the bone.
On section 2-S. 121 amended:
Will the minister explain the effect of putting 123 under the same classification as 122?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Putting 123 in clause 121 will bring public elevators in the East under the same supervision and control of the Grain Board as those in the West and as terminal elevators are under. A public

elevator, as my hon. friend knows, is one that receives for storage and transit grain which has been certificated at Fort William, and which passes through on its way to the ultimate market. It has been felt for a number of years, and the Grain Commission have been very insistent on this, that there should be more supervision and control over the grain after it leaves Fort William and until it reaches the seaboard. The purpose of the inclusion of section 123 in clause 121 is simply to give the same authority and supervision and control over the eastern public elevator as there is over the terminal elevator. The purpose is to endeavour to keep intact the quality of the grain as it is certificated at Fort William or Port Arthur until it reaches the ultimate market.

As I understand the section reads:
No person owning, managing, operating or otherwise interested in a terminal elevator shall huy or sell grain at any point in the eastern or western inspection division.
As I understand, if this clause is adopted owners of public elevators will come under this prohibition, they will be deprived of the privilege which they now have of buying grain in the western division. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-exception in case of terminal elevators:

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Section 3 is simply the exception of terminal elevators from the car clause. It would be impossible to carry on the work of a terminal elevator at Fort William under the restriction of the car clause. The clause that will govern them will be No. 133.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.
On section 3-terminal elevators:

The section which, of course, is really an amendment to the be-gining of section 195, and which is called 194a, provides that:
The provisions of sections 195 to 207, both inclusive, shall not apply to elevators licensed as terminal elevators.
I suppose the minister intends to make the elevators at Moosejaw and Saskatoon terminal elevators under a declaration by Order in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They must be terminal elevators.

In paragraph y of the
interpretation section it is provided that:
Terminal elevator includes every elevator or warehouse which receives or ships grain and is located at any point declared by the Governor in Council to be a terminal.
Under this section 3 there is nothing to prevent every elevator at Saskatoon and Moosejaw becoming terminal elevators because every elevator, just as well as the Government elevator, will be an elevator which receives and ships grain and is situated at a point declared by the Governor in Council to be a terminal. The Governor in Council will declare Saskatoon and Moose-jaw to be terminal points and this clause says then that every elevator which is situated at these points shall be a terminal elevator. Consequently, it would look as if the local elevators in Moosejaw and Saskatoon would hot come under sections 195 to 207, namely, the clauses in regard to cars and the car order book.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think there is a point in that which I did not notice. I would suggest that we pass the clause and I will not push the Bill to the third reading, but I will have this matter looked into so that if anything is necessary to guard it I can introduce it as an amendment.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Louis Coderre (Minister of Mines), the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to regulate and control the manufacture, importation and use of explosives and the construction, licensing and inspection of premises used for the manufacture and storing of explosives, and to provide for the making of inquiries where an accidental explosion has occurred.

This is a resolution that, no doubt, is important, and there are a number of members who would like to be informed in regard to it. There are very few in the House just now and we do not wish to delay the business, but if the minister will make a full explanation on the second reading of the Bill there will be no objection to it going through without the information being given now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will do that.

I would ask the hon.
the minister if this resolution contemplates the avoidance of such accidents as happened a year or two ago at Beloeil? There was a powder manufactory at Beloeil and an explosion took place with the result that ten persons were killed. There is another powder manufactory on lie Perrot. It is quite near the track, and I am often nervous when I pass that point on my way to Montreal. Does this Bill contemplate circumstances of that nature?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I shall be pleased, as
requested by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), to delay the full explanation of this proposal until the second reading of the Bill. I would say to my hon. colleague from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) that this resolution is to authorize the regulation and control of the manufacture, storage, testing, importation and transportation of explosives generally and the Bill which will be founded upon it proposes to do away, as far as possible, with such accidents as the one which he has mentioned. This is a most important measure. It should have been passed years ago. I remember that in 1911, my predecessor, Mr. COMMONS
Templeman, brought a Bill before the House, a few clauses of which were passed. The accident which has been alluded to by my hon. friend from Rouville is not the only one that has occurred during the past year. I have here a list, based on information we have obtained from the Labour Gazette, of ninety-two fatal accidents in 1913 due to explosion in mining, railway construction and other employments.
The present Bill will deal with such conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I think so.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. CODERRE thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 189, to regulate the manufacture, testing, storage, and importation of explosives.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), Bill No. 180, to amend the Canada Temperance Act, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The first purpose of the Bill is to make the Canada Temperance Act of practical application in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. The second purpose of the Bill is to obviate a difficutly which has arisen in connection with elections under the Canada Temperance Act in the unorganized territories of Ontario. The law at present says that the persons entitled to vote upon an election for the adoption of the Canada Temperance Act, are the persons who would be entitled to vote in Dominion elections, and in order to hold an election under the Canada Temperance Act it is necessary that there should be a list in force for the purpose of a Dominion election. The law provides that in the unorganized territories an electoral list shall be made every year unless the Governor in Council dispenses with the making of such list, and it has been usual for the Governor in Council to so dispense with the making of the list in years other than that in which a general election is anticipated. Consequently, in certain cases it was necessary to make a special list for an election for the adoption of the Canada Temperance Act, and inasmuch as the list so made must be suitable for use at a Dominion election, even where

only a small part of the riding would be included in the district in which it was sought to bring the Canada Temperance Act into force, it was found to be necessary to make a list for the entire riding. This entailed additional and useless expense, and the purpose of the amendment is to provide that in such case the list may be made to cover only that part of any riding included in the district in which the Temperance Act is sought to be brought into force. It is provided that such list shall be applicable for the purposes of that election only, and shall not be used in the event of a Dominion election becoming necessary in that riding. It was considered undesirable that in a Dominion election in the riding part of the list should be made at one time and part at another.
It is farther sought to amend the law so as to remove doubt as to the jurisdiction of the Superior Courts to hear contestations of the validity of elections held under the Canada Temperance Act. I would not be inclined to think that the doubt as to the jurisdiction was very serious, but as the question had arisen it was thought wise to remove any doubt. In connection with the lists there was also found another difficulty which is sought to be remedied by an amendment which I intend to propose to the Bill as introduced. The Canada Temperance Act provides that twenty-five per cent of the qualified voters shall petition for the ordering of an election under the Act. In districts composed partly of organized and partly of unorganized territory, difficulty has arisen from the fact that in the unorganized territory there was not in force in certain cases any list of electors Which would enable the Secretary of State to determine whether or not the petitioners were twenty-five per cent of the electors in that unorganized territory. The amendment will provide that in such case, for the purpose of determining whether or not there are twenty-five per cent of the voters in the unorganized territories who have signed the petition, the Secretary of State shall take the number of voters who were on the last list in force in that territory as being the number whereof twenty-five per cent must sign the petition. This is made subject to the. exception that in cases where it may be demonstrated that there has been a noted diminution in the population of the unorganized district since the making of the last list, then twenty-five per cent of the persons who can be shown to be living in the district will be sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the Act as it now stands provides for separate elections in cities and counties. The difficulty that arose in the western provinces was that there were no subdivisions of territory corresponding with the (districts in which the Act provided that a temperance election might be held. The way in which that difficulty is sought to be obviated is by a provision that in those provinces the word ' county ' shall mean a riding for a Dominion election. It makes the Act applicable, and at the same time obviates any difficulty about the lists, because a county for the purposes of the Canada Temperance Act will be the county for the purpose of a Dominion election, and naturally the same voters' list will be applicable.
Will the minister tell the House in how many counties in the Dominion the Canada Temperance Act is now in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in a position to give that information. Perhaps I should have anticipated that question, but I did not anticipate it.

Can the minister tell me whether my information is correct or not? I am informed that, say in a county in the province of Ontario, in which there is a small city and a large rural vote, in the city there may be a majority of people who do not approve of the bringing of this Act into operation, while in the rural district there may be a large majority approving of it. In such a case will the rural people have the power to impose their wishes on the urban people?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps the best way to answer the hon. member is to give him the definition in the statute. Under section 2, the interpretation section of the Act as it stands, we have this provision, which I think answers the question:
In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, ' county ' includes every town, township, parish and other division or municipality, except a city, within the territorial limits of the county, and also a union of counties united for municipal purposes.
I should say that under that provision, in an election held for a county, which includes a city, the city would not be included in the county.
But a town would?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, a town would.
Everything that was not a city would be included.
The amendment in regard to the provinces in the West will be subject to the same exception; or, in other words, our cities in Saskatchewan will be masters of their own destinies in this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid that the amendment as drawn will not meet that requirement. The provision in this Bill is that:
As respects the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, ' county' means the electoral districts therein as designated by the Representation Act.
In that respect this definition differs from the definition of the word ' county ' as given generally. That, however, is already the law as regards the province of Manitoba. The present provision of the law as respects the province of Manitoba is:
* County ' means the electoral districts therein as designated by the Representation Act.
And we are now making applicable to Alberta and Saskatchewan the law as it stands with regard to Manitoba. If the hon. member thinks it desirable to make the same distinction with regard to these provinces, I am quite prepared to consider his suggestion.

I am not very familiar with the matter; the minister knows it better than I do; but if we are thoughtlessly making one law for Ontario and another law for Saskatchewan, we may be in error. On the face of it, I have grave doubts whether it will be in the interest of temperance, say in the West, where we have a very large rural population, if we ean take a constituency including a city, because the city may consider that the prohibition of liquor is not desirable, and that it can not be successfully operated, whereas the county people may hold the opposite view, and may be able to impose their views on the city. I am not at the moment placing myself on record either as in favour of the amendment or as against it; but if we are making legislation for one province different from that in another we should do so knowing that we are doing it and why we do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a question of assimilating the law in Saskatchewan and Alberta to that in force in Manitoba. At first glance one might be inclined to think that conditions in Alberta and Saskatchewan might be more similar to those in Manitoba than possibly to those in Ontario. I have not heard any suggestion that the law does not operate satisfactorily in the province of Manitoba, and I think that the same provision under the Act is applicable to British Columbia.
British Columbia has a very small rural settlement as compared with Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
