speechtext: If the hon. member, who is no doubt more familiar with the conditions in these two western provinces than I can pretend to be, thinks there will be a material advantage in assimilating the law in these two provinces to the law in force in Ontario, rather than to the law as in force in Manitoba, I shall be glad to consider the suggestion.

I am not speaking after very much reflection; but I am rather inclined to think that what the minister suggests may be my view, so far as I can see now. The fact that Manitoba has a certain condition of affairs does not seem to be a strong argument why the law in force in Manitoba should be applicable to Saskatchewan. In fact, I would rather follow Ontario in this matter than Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The mere fact that a certain provision is in force in Manitoba is not a reason why it should be put into force in Saskatchewan, unless it appears that the provision as regards Manitoba is more suitable to Saskatchewan than the provision as regards Ontario. As I said a moment ago, at first glance one would be inclined to think that conditions in Saskatchewan and Alberta would be more similar to conditions in Manitoba than to conditions in Ontario. When the law was originally made with this distinction, I presume there must have been some reason for the difference, and I have not heard any representation upon the subject indicating any desire that we should differentiate between the law as applicable to Manitoba and the law as applicable to the other prov-' inces. I do not want to be understood as saying that because it is so in Manitoba, it should be so in Saskatchewan and Alberta. It is entirely a question of what is most suitable for the two provinces.

Would the word ' county ' have the same meaning in the East

as in the West ? It is possible that this little discussion may be due to the minister's having given in his kindness an answer without giving the matter very much consideration. I am not sure that there is a difference. I asked the minister to put it beyond peradventure. I wonidered if the minister had looked into it carefully enough to be positive in his opinion that a different condition of affairs does prevail in Manitoba from that in Ontario. I know that there is a debate on the subject. If the minister is sure on that point, I will let it rest; but if he gave a somewhat hurried answer, there may be an explanation, and even the Manitoba cities are the governors.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
In my judgment, the provision which is applicable in Ontario whereby the city is excluded would be properly applicable in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

A city is incorporated by the provincial authority, and given independent powers lor what seem good and sufficient reasons. The fact that it has been created a city, the fact that a certain place has been created a city by the provincial authority, means that the provincial authority desires to establish a separate control within that area; and it seems to me that it would be rather a mistake to ignore that plain intent of the provincial authority when creating a city. I would suggest that in applying the law to the electoral districts, the same exception be made as regards cities in Alberta and Saskatchewan as is made un-. ^questionably in regard to Ontario and probably in regard to Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall look into the question, as I mentioned a moment ago. The definition of county which excludes the cities is not specially applicable to Ontario, but is a general definition. Then, we have provision with regard to Ontario, with regard to Manitoba, and with regard to British Columbia, and we shall have with regard to Saskatchewan an'd Alberta.
I think it is quite possible that one should read the definition as applicable to all these specified cases, in which event the exception	of the	cities would be
general.	I confess I did not consider any question arising except that we should make this law applicable and workable in the two provinces. If we reach the conclusion that it is applicable, the Bill might stand as it is; if we reach a contrary conclusion upon what is represented, I dlo not see any objection to modifying the Bill so as to make the exclusion of the cities apply.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I was not
present when this debate commenced, but 1 heard the hon. minister speak on the introduction of the Bill. So far as- he has spoken, he has not given any information as to the raison d'etre of this Bill. Are we to understand that this Bill is asked for by the temperance organizations, or is there any demand in the western provinces for the change of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before the right hon.
gentleman came in I had endeavoured to explain the reasons that brought about the proposal of these amendments. It has been represented by people interested in the tem-Iperance cause that the Act was not workable in Saskatchewan, and if I am not mistaken the hon. member for Edmonton <Mr. Oliver) but a few days ago referred
in this House to this lack of provision in the Act making it workable in these two provinces. It is because it appears to us fair and right that a law intended to be of general application, and unworkable in these particular provinces simply for want of definition of those counties or districts in which the Act might be brought into force, ought to be so modified as to make it applicable throughout the country generally. The other amendments suggested in the Bill are the result not so much of representation from anybody as of difficulties that arise in the application of the Act and that have caused a great deal of trouble. One difficulty was to get a list for the purpose of an election necessary for the adoption of the Canada Temperance Act, where the whole or part-more particularly where part of the counties in which the election was sought to be held consisted of unorganized territory in the province of Ontario. As I explained, it was found that under the law as it stands, in virtue whereof persons entitled to vote in an election on the Canada Temperance Act are described as persons who would be entitled to vote at a Dominion election to be held at the same time, wherever a county for the purpose of the Canada Temperance Act included some part of an unorganized territory in the province of Ontario, the only method by which you could get a list applicable to that part which was comprised of unorganized territory was by making a list under the Dominion Elections Act, and it was considered, after careful examination, that you could only make a list for the purpose of the Dominion Elections Act by making a list for the entire Dominion riding. So that where, perhaps, but one-tenth part of the Dominion riding forming part of the county for the purposes of a Canada Temperance Act election consisted of unorganized territory, we were under the necessity of making a list for the entire riding, which entailed a very considerable useless expense. That was one difficulty. A second difficulty that arose also related to the unorganized territory-that in order that an election should be held in a county as it is defined in this Act, it is required that there should be a petition made by twenty dive per cent of the qualified voters. In that connection the difficulty was that where the county for temperance election purposes consisted partly of organized and partly of unorganized territory, we found ourselves in this position; when the peti-

tioner presented his petition it was easy enough to ascertain whether he had twenty-five per cent of the voters in the organized territory, because there was a list to which he could refer, but with regard to the unorganized territory it was exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, for the petitioner satisfactorily to establish that he had twenty-five per cent of the persons who would be entitled to vote at that temperance election when it came on, because the lists, being made only for the purposes of that temperance election, naturally would not be made until after the occasion for it had been shown by the presentation and granting of the petition for the election. It is mainly on account of the difficulties which I have mentioned with regard to the unorganized territory that the decision was arrived at to amend the Act. When we had decided to amend the Act, it was pointed out that in its present condition, as I mentioned a little while ago, it was not workable in these two provinces and we thought that we ought to meet that difficulty.

In the preparation of this
Act, has the minister taken into consideration the representations that were made to him in March, 1913, by Dr. Bazin, of Orms-town, representing the Temperance Association in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The representations
made by Dr. Bazin have certainly had the consideration which they deserved, both on account of their intrinsic merits and on account of the source from which they came. But the principal suggestion of Dr. Bazin looked to a much more fundamental amendment of this Act than anything which is suggested here. In fact, one could hardly call it an amendment to the Act; it was the suggestion of an entirely new procedure with regard to the adoption of the Canada Temperance Act. I am speaking now solely from memory, but I do not think that I am mistaken. The principal suggestion of Dr. Bazin was that at every general election we should simultaneously submit, all over the country, I understand, the question whether the Dominion Temperance Act, or prohibition in some shape; should be adopted. That, of course, is a proposition that, I think, calls for more serious consideration than any of the amendments which it is now proposed to make to the Act, which look merely to the making of the Act more workable than it is under present conditions.

I would like to bring
to the attention of the minister what seems 
to me to ibe an anomaly in the Act. Any city situated in a county which brings the Canada Temperance Act into force is excluded from the operation of the Act, but if a municipality should receive a city charter after the coming into force of the Act, the newly-created city is in the same position as the Whole county and is not excluded from the operation of the Act. If it is the intention of the legislation to exclude all cities from the operation of the Act, the Act should be amended to provide that when a civic corporation receives a * city charter after the coming into force of the Act in the county in Which it is situated, that city shall be excluded from the operation of the Act. The Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, on certiorari application, decided that civic institutions receiving city charters after the coming into force of the Act in the county in which it was situated, should come within the operation of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not understand
that the Canada Temperance Act provides that you cannot pass it in a city. What it provides is that when you pass it in a county the city shall be excepted, but the city may pass the Act for itself. The purpose is not to say that the Scott Act shall never be enforced in any city; the purpose is to prevent cities from being controlled by the rest of the county in which they are situated.

But that is not exactly the point I am making. The Act as it now stands provides that when the Canada Temperance Act is brought into force in a county in which there is a city, that city is excluded from the operation of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is provided that the city shall not be bound by the proceedings and the voting of the county.

Exactly so. If a town
receives a city charter after the county in which the city is situate is brought under the operation of the Act, the Act does not apply to that city. I think there should be something in the Act to make its application uniform in respect of cities growing up in counties in which the Canada Temperance Act is put in force. The mere fact that the county has voted to bring itself within the operation of the Canada Temperance Act should not provide that the Act shall apply also to a town which afterwards receives a city charter, especially in view of the fact that that town would be exempt from

its operation if it were a city at the time the county came undeT the operation of the Canada Temperance Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It may, perhaps, be desirable to make some provision to enable the city to be included in the country, because it has become a city, to withdraw itself from the operation of the Act, but I do not quite see that because something that was part of a county at the time the election was held, and therefore bound, as part of the county, by the result of the election in the county, should, by the mere fact that it becomes a city, cease to be under the operation of the Act. That would be a proposition which, I think, ought to be acceded to if the provision of the law was that the Act was never to apply in cities. But that, as I understand it, is not the provision of the law. The Act may be enforced in cities if it is properly brought into force. Where the Act has been properly 'brought into force in a territory which at the time is not a city; but which subsequently becomes a city, the fact that that portion of the territory has become a city does not alter the fact that the Temperance Act has been properly brought into force within it. Whether, because it has become a city, it should be given some exceptional method of relieving itself of the condition with regard to the Temperance Act in which it was before it became a city is, no doubt, a matter that deserves consideration, but it does not, at first glance, seem to me that it goes without saying that merely because it has become a city, it ought to be relieved from a condition which it, in common with the rest of the county, had imposed upon itself.

I would think that there is no provision in the Act which would allow that new city, which received its charter after the Act came into force in the county, to exempt itself from the operation of the Act. There is where the difficulty comes in. If it were the intention of the Act to have one law for the city and another for the county or to give the city 'the option of having the law, no matter what the county may decide, there should be something in the Act to provide for new cities that may arise. I am arguing the matter merely from the standpoint of uniformity in the law. In the city to which I have special reference they could not bring into operation a license system as the Act stands now. They would have to be bound by the action of the county when it had perhaps one-third the population of the city to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will realize that his suggestion has no direct relation to the amendment sought to be made, and I have to confess it is the first time that that matter has been brought to my attention. I would require to consider it further before determining whether or not legislation should be introduced to meet the difficulty. The present amendment looks simply to providing voters' lists and to making the Act workable in provinces in which it is not now workable.
I shall be very glad to consider the suggestion made and see whether it really calls for a remedy, and what would be the proper remedy.

We might take it for
granted that, in a county in Ontario, Quebec, or any province where there are counties, or in a eonstitutncy in the western provinces, where the Act has been brought into force, the city included in the county had voted in favour of the Act. But, if not, the city would have its own remedy: it could get up a petition and have a revote.
It could not.

In that way it could
take itself from under the jurisdiction o>f the Act. If that is not possible, an amendment to the Act giving that power could easily be drafted. I do not think, however, that any town should be able to remove itself from the operation of the Act simply by forming itself into a city. A certain population should be defined for a city. In the West, for instance, we know of certain places of two thousand population suddenly becoming cities.

Five thousand is the
law.

I would refer my hon.
friend to Weyburn, which has only two or three thousand.
That is a place of seven thousand.
If we are going into this system, it should be confined to cities Of ten thousand population.

Subsection (c) of clause 2, reads:
In the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, in any registry office or in any sheriff's office in the respective electoral districts.
I suppose that is in relation to the posting of notices in connection with the holding of elections. In Alberta and Sas-

katchewan there are a number of electoral districts in which there is no sheriff's office, or registry office, and some other provision must be made to meet that case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is there not
4 p.m. a sheriff in each county?
These are Dominion electoral districts, in some of which there is no sheriff.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I realize the difficulty, and would be very glad to meet it. What is desired is to get some place where notices could be posted where they would get the greatest possible publicity. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could help me in this regard.

I think the matter
would have to be left to the decision of the officer o*f the Dominion Government. I do not know of any office that you could depend on being located in any particular constituency that would have particular prominence. A Dominion lands sub-office would be quite prominent, but there might be constituencies in which there would not be one.

In regard to the
clause providing for the electoral districts being designated as counties for the purposes of this Act, I would point out that under redistribution, if it goes into effect, cities in western Canada will be divided. We shall have Calgary east and west and Edmonton east and west. This measure might be adopted in the east half of the city, which would go dry, while the other part of the city would remain wet. How would the minister deal with a case like that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If, on more careful examination, the conclusion should be reached that the city is included in the county for purposes of this Act as the law now stands, I shall amend this Bill so as to exclude the city and let the city in these provinces stand, as in the other provinces, as a distinct entity by itself, which, as such distinct entity, will adopt or not adopt the Act upon its own decision.

Will the hon. Minister
of Justice confine that to cities with 10,000 of a population?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In regard to our making a modification as to the population of cities which should be excluded from the counties, that is another proposition which looks to modify what I might call the substance of the Canada Temperance Act. I have not

considered that question at all. These amendments in the procedure of the Canada Temperance Act were urged upon us as being immediately necessary. We have not had any suggestion in regard to what population should be necessary to exclude a city. It seems to be evident that we shall not be able to finish the Bill without a further consideration and I shall be very glad to consider the suggestion and see if it is possible to comply with it. It has been suggested to me that permission to post the notice in a post office might meet the point which has been raised.

Yes, the post office will
be all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We might add ' or in any registry office, or in any sheriff's office or, failing such, in any post office'. I suppose it will be preferable that where there is a registry or sheriff's office it should be posted there?
Yes.

I think it would be
better where there is no registry or sheriff's office that the petition should be sent simply to the Secretary of State and let him direct the place where it shall be posted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We might provide that it shall be posted as may be designated by the Secretary of State.
Let the man simply send his petition to the Secretary of State, and let the Secretary of State say as to the posting of the notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would think that suggestion better than the one in regard to the post office. I shall try to make an amendment to meet that. I beg to move that section 2 be amended by adding at the end of subsection c, the following:
Or, if there be no such registry office or sheriff's office, then in such place as may be designated by the Secretary of State for the purpose.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 5-publication of notice in newspaper:

Why does it prescribe
that the notice shall be published in a newspaper ' at or near ' the city? Why not say ' in ' the city?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We can almost absolutely count on every city having a paper, but it must be drafted to meet the possible case of the paper not being published

actually in the city. I do not know that we can take it for granted that all our cities have newspapers; they certainly ought to have.

Legally, suppose a man puts the notice in a newspaper published fifty miles from a city; would that be near the city? Under this Act he is not compelled to put it in a newspaper published in the city; he could put it in a paper published elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There would "be no
objection to amending it so as to provide that it must be published in a paper in the city.
If there be one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If there be one, or if
there be not one, then in the nearest place. I would move that section 5 be amended by striking out the words ' at or near ' in the 41st line and substituting the word.' in '.

I presume that this Act may be submitted to the electors in municipalities in which there is no newspaper published, and I think the notice ought to be in some newspaper in the county or district in which the vote is taking place even although it is not near the city. I think that the nearest newspaper ought to have the opportunity of publishing this notice if it is going to be of any benefit to the electors.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The intention is that
the notice of the contestation of the election shall be published for two weeks in two newspapers published at or near the city or the county in' which the vote has taken place, or if there be no newspaper published in such city or county, then in the nearest newspaper. I move:
That the section he amended by inserting in the forty-second line, after the word ' place,' the words:
Or If there be but one newspaper published in the city or county then in that newspaper, and in a newspaper whose place of publication is nearest the said city or county; or if there be no newspaper published In said city or county, then in two newspapers whose place or places of publication are nearest said city or county.

The section does not say in what language the notice should be published. In provinces in which the English and French languages are official, I suppose the notice should be published in both languages.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is a reasonable suggestion. We might perhaps say that in
the province of Quebec it should be published in both languages.
In Manitoba both languages are official.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would move that the following words be added to the amendment:
Such publication to be made in the French and English languages In cities or counties wherein there is a newspaper published in each of these languages.
Section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that the Bill be amended by inserting in section 2 the following subsections:
2.	If in any city or county or any part thereof there are no voters' lists which could be used for the purpose of this Act, the petition shall have appended to it the genuine signatures of one-fourth in number of such persons as are voters or who possess the qualifications of voters, other than being on the voters' lists, for such city or county.
3.	For the purposes of this section the number of voters in any city or county in which or in any part of which there are no voters' lists which could be used for the purposes of this Act shall be:
(a)	Where there are voters' lists in force for part of such city or county, the number of voters on such lists, together with the number of voters who were on the last voters' lists that were in force in the rest of such city or county;
(b)	Where there are no voters' lists in force in such city or county, then the number of voters that were in the last voters' lists that were in force in such a city or county; or
(c)	Where there are no voters' lists in force in the whole or any part of any city or county, such number as is established to the satisfaction of the Secretary of State as being the total number of persons who possess the qualifications of voters for such city or county, other than that of being on a voters' list.
The purpose of this amendment is to meet the situation where the Secretary of State has to determine whether he has 25 per cent of the voters who have signed the petition, and where in whole or in part there is no voters' lists for the districts in 'which the election is to be held. In the case where the absence of the voters' list is only partial, he is to take as the total number of voters the total number of voters cn the existing voters' lists, plus the total number of voters that were on the last existing voters' list for the portion or district of the county for which there is no voters' list. Where there are no voters' lists for the whole of the county, he takes the number of the voters that were on the last voters' lists. Finally, as an alternative to that, if there be reason for it, he may take what is proved otherwise to be 25 per

cent of the people who are actually entitled to vote. The purpose is to avoid the necessity of this last requirement in all cases, and to facilitate the establishment of the 25 per cent wherever it can be done by reference to the last existing voters' lists.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg to move to amend the Bill further by adding to section 5 at the end thereof the following:
No such action shall be commenced until the plaintiff has given security for costs to the satisfaction of the court in which he proposes to bring his action, and no such action shall be brought after the expiration of one year from the date of the polling.
This is the requirement that any person contesting the election shall give security for costs to the satisfaction of the court, and furthermore to put a limit of time within which the contestation may (be made.

Does not the minister
think a year is a little long?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not quite sure
but that it is a little long.

I think six months is

stagedirection
speechtext:
The House again in .Committee on Bill No. 138, to amend the Irrigation Act.-Mr. Roche. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 5-minister may permit diversion of water:

It has been pointed
out to me that this clause will affect certain litigation between the users of the Canadian Pacific Railway irrigation ditch in the vicinity of Strathmore in their action against the Canadian Pacific Railway Irrigation Company. The reason is that this legislation is made retroactive. I have been asked to urge upon the minister that the users of water should stil-l be given the privilege of carrying on their action against the company. In this connection I might read a letter which I have received which probably will explain the case a little more clearly than I can. This is from the chairman of the Test Case Committee. As the minister knows there has been a good deal of difficulty in that part of the country with the Canadian Pacific Railway Irrigation Company:
You will notice on page 3, '20 F,' provisions for the minister being permitted to issue permits to persons or companies to divert and use water during the construction period, and in section 15 it provides for actions applying to all cases where the minister has given permits, which it appears to me is to authorize what the minister has already done which had not previously been authorized.
Now, they want to avoid that, they ask to be left to fight out their dispute without any retroactive legislation-that is they do not want to have their interest impaired in any way by this proposed measure, and they claim that it will interfere with their

interest in that respect. There is a good deal of strong feeling in that district over the treatment received by the farmers who have purchased land from the Canadian Pacific Railway Irrigation Company. As the minister know.s, there has been difficulty over the reclassification of land. It is held that under the proposed reclassification that the farmers may be compelled to pay more than they should for the land .they bought. This land that they bought was guaranteed to be irrigable, and they claim that, under the terms of the reclassification arrangement, lands which have proven to be nonirrigable, but which were sold as irrigable and subject to irrigation from the time they were purchased, they will have to pay for at as high as $8 an acre, in addition to additional price. It has been represented to me, and I would like to place it before the minister, that this difficulty is serious in that particular district. There is a great deal o.f feeling and a great deal of dissatisfaction. The demand is made by the Grievance Committee in that district that there should be a Royal Commission to investigate the charges made by the farmers against the Irrigation Company before the Government takes any action in regard to the reclassification of the land. It is also pointed out to me that officials of the department are .addressing letters to farmers in that district advising them that it is in their best interests to sign up a new contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Irrigation Company, in which there are provisions with regard to reclassification which would bring about further charges upon the farmer. Of course, the company has its own side of the ease-that the lands are satisfactory and the terms of sale are being carried out. But it has been represented to me by practical iTrigationists, who have been in that district since the commencement of irrigation farming, that the condition of things was misrepresented, and that, under the proposed reclassification, they will be compelled to pay $8 more for their land, which it was claimed was irrigable land. I bring this to the attention of the minister, because this clause is objected to by the Test Case Committee. They prefer to be left in a position to carry on any .action they may bring against the Irrigation Company, and they say that section would interfere with their rights.

It is not intended at all that this Bill should interfere in the slightest degree with those who have tracts from the Canadian Pacific Railway Irrigation Company, and I do not see how such an interpretation could be placed upon it. On the other hand, there have been instances where it would have been a very great hardship to have denied to an irrigation company-I am not now referring to the Canadian Pacific Railway Irrigation Company-the privilege of using a portion of their works before the completion of those works in their entirety. I am aware that considerable difficulty has arisen between the Canadian Pacific railway and the water users in the Canadian Pacific Railway irrigation tract. The matter was brought to my attention about a year ago. Representatives both of the company and of the farmers met me, and I decided, after hearing their representations, that it would be the part of wisdom that we should have a reclassification of those lands to see whether they were actually irrigable or not. At first the company protested strongly, and did not wish to submit to such reclassification. At that time the chief demand made upon the Government was either to institute an inquiry or have a reclassification of the land. We are now having a reclassification of these lands, the company having decided to submit to the request. The work of reclassification is being conducted by their officials as well as by engineers on behalf of the Government. This Bill will not interfere with any test case going on in the courts. For, as a matter of fact and practice, ever since the Act was put into effect in 1894, parties have been allowed to use their partially constructed works without taking out a license. This Bill is simply to legalize what has been done as a matter of practice hitherto. I may quote illustrations furnished me by the department to show the benefit arising from allowing an irrigation company to irrigate land before their entire works are completed.
Some years ago, in the early history of Moosejaw, that city obtained its water supply from Moosejaw creek, which flows through the city. This supply was never of a satisfactory quality, and finally became insufficient in quantity as well. Application was made by the city for permission to take a further supply from springs removed several miles from the city. This application was made in June, 1908. Authorization to construct the works



was issued in 1913, subject to the acquisition of the necessary right of way by the city. The city authorities	constructed
their works in	advance	of	thisauthorization, but	secured	only	partof the required	right	of	way.
It was absolutely necessary for the city to have a further supply of water from this particular source as soon as their works were sufficiently constructed to enable them to lay a pipe from this creek. No objection was made by the Government of the day or by this Government. The city has not as yet received a license to use the water from this source, solely owing to the fact that they have not as yet been able to secure their entire right of way. Nevertheless, they have been using water from this source during the last four years. The same thing is being done in connection with its water supply from Sandy Creek, near Caron. In this case the works are not yet completed, but so great has been the need of water that the partially completed works have been in use for some time, although, as yet, unlicensed. I could cite many other illustrations to show what a hardship . it would be to prevent a permit being issued until the licenses were granted after the completion of the work. I can assure hon. gentlemen that it is not intended to interfere at all with any decision that may be given with regard to any test case that is now pending.

Looking over the correspondence which the hon. member for Medicine Hat has here, I see that it is the opinion of counsel that this legislation would interfere with a case now pending. Would there be any objection to putting a saving clause in the section, saying that it would not interfere with any litigation now in progress?
I have no objection to that.

The counsel for the
people to whom I refer have made this statement:
Disputes exist between the railway company and the users respecting the obligations of the users of water heretofore used and as this legislation is retroactive, the rights and liabilities that exist between the railway company and the users would be affected.
I sent a copy of the printed Bill to the committee and to the counsel, who makes this statement in a letter to the committee.

I think the objections urged would be removed by adding to section 5 the words:

But shall not apply to any case with respect to which litigation is now pending.

I am not familiar with the Act, but I would point out to my hon. friend that where a clause of that kind is inserted in a Bill, the wording usually runs this way:
Nothing in this Act shall apply to any case with respect to which litigation is now pending.
The amendment suggested by my hon. friend says that nothing in this section shall apply to pending litigation, but there might be something in some other part of the Act which would militate against litigation now pending. If it is the intention of the minister that nothing in the Act shall apply to pending litigation, it is better to say so, and to make the provision to that effect the last clause in the Bill.
Any litigation now pending is subject to the existing Act. If we say that nothing in this Act shall apply to any litigation, I am afraid we would be going a little too far.

That is not what I
mean. I am talking about the Bill now before the committee; the hon. minister is referring to the original Act as amended. The hon. minister might make his amendment read: ' Nothing in the amending Act; ' that would make the matter perfectly clear.
I have no objection to such an amendment.

May I suggest to the
minister that the amendment as now proposed to this particular section should come in at the end of the Act?
All right.

I have here a statement from Mr. Henry Sorensen, of Strathmore, who is chairman of the Farmers' Combined Irrigation Committee, with regard to the reclassification of land. It is as follows:
With regard to the reclassification as it is now being conducted you will notice in the document, which the farmers have been asked to sign, pledging themselves to accept the reclassification as it is being conducted by the Government, that each farmer will be asked to incur an additional expense of $8 per acre for drainage and other work in connection with the lands.
Now this means in plain words nothing else but: that after the Canadian Pacific railway have charged men an exorbitant price for so-called irrigation lands and after the water has so deteriorated the soil that the lands are unfit for farming purposes the farmers are now to be put to an additional expense of $8 per acre to endeavour to put the lands into the same con-

dition as they were prior to being spoiled by the water.
That is the statement he makes in connection with reclassification, a statement which has also been made in other letters which I have received from the farmers of that district-that under this reclassification there will be an extra charge on certain of their lands of $8 per acre. I have here the forms of an agreement and a letter from the Superintendent of Irrigation under date of February 23, to a farmer in that district, which reads:
Department of the Interior.
Canada.
Ottawa, February 23, 1914.
Sir:
According to records filed in this department by the Canadian Pacmc Railway Company, you have purchased from that company certain irrigable and non-irrigable land and have entered into an agreement with the company for the supply by it to you of water for the irrigation of the irrigable land so purchased.
The company has informed this department of the completion of the works for the irrigation of the western section of its irrigation tract and has asked for the issue of a water license. The Minister of the Interior has decided that, before the works as constructed can be accepted and before any water license can properly be issued in the company's favour, it will be necessary for the company's classification of alleged irrigable land to be checked and, where necessary, revised by departmental officials. The company will be required to file with the Commissioner of Irrigation such additional plans and other data as may be required by him in connection with the reclassification. When such plans have been filed the commissioner will have such examination made on the ground as may be necessary to determine the accuracy of the plans and where necessary will have a resurvey made. The company's classification will then be carefully checked and, if necessary, revised.
The company has agreed to accept and abide by the result of such reclassification and, to amend and adjust all its sales-contracts and water agreements in accordance therewith. I am, therefore, to request you to state whether or not you are willing to similarly accept the result of the reclassification to De made under the direction of the Minister of Interior. There is no desire on the part of this department to interfere in any way with any rights which you may now possess under your existing contracts with the company and no effort will be made to induce you to sign any agreement against your own inclination. It is believed, however, that the signing of such an agreement will materially facilitate the settlement of the existing difficulties between the company and lessees of water.
The attached form of agreement is believed to correctly show the lands purchased by you from the said company and the essential facts in connection with your agreement to receive water from it for irrigation purposes. If you are prepared to accept the result of the reclassification of land to be made under the direction of the minister, I am to request you 2271
to sign and return to me at your very earliest convenience the form of agreement attached hereto, retaining one copy thereof. Tour signature should be properly witnessed and sealed. Kindly advise me of your decision in this matter at your very earliest convenience.
Tour obedient servant,
E. F. Drake,
Superintendent of Irrigation.
What was pointed out to me in connection with this letter was that the farmers object to the reclassification, that their demand has been for a Royal Commission to investigate the whole situation prior to any reclassification. I am now speaking of this particular association, and I would not say that this includes all the farmers of that particular irrigation tract.
5 p.m. I would again ask the minister if the case for a Royal Commission has been presented to him, and what decision he has come to in regard to it; and also whether the statement made here that this reclassification will mean an additional expenditure of $8 an acre to put the lands ' in the condition in which they were prior to being spoiled by water/ is correct. I may say that I know nothing about the case myself except what is in the letters I have received.

ing to influence the farmers. As a matter of fact, the letter distinctly states that the Government are not in any way trying to influence them. It is erroneous to say that by reason of the reclassification they will be called upon to pay $8 more an acre for their lands. They have their contracts with the Canadian Pacific railway. We have asked the company not to prosecute any litigation against any water users in arrears for rental until after a reclassification has been made. The company strongly objected to that, but we have impressed them with the necessity of foregoing action against the farmers pending the reclassification. The result has been that there have been no proceedings against the farmers. This will not mean an increase of $8 an acre for the land. If it is found that the Canadian Pacific railway's original classification was right, I presume the farmers will be subject to their contracts with the Canadian Pacific railway, whatever they agreed to pay for the land. If it is found that the lands have been wrongly classified, there will have to be a rearrangement and a new contract. It was for that reason that the letter was sent out. The Royal Commission which has been recently asked for, was not originally asked for; in fact, it was only asked for after the reclassification was under way. Very many of these farmers have agreed to sign an agreement that they will abide by the reclassification, probably in the proportion of three to one.

Could the minister say
what seems to be the reason this writer has for saying that a reclassification will mean an increase in the cost of the land? As the minister explained, the man is simply writing nonsense, but surely he must have had some foundation upon which to base the idea.

Supposing they have a
contract with the Canadian Pacific railway to purchase lands that are supposed to be irrigable and that the contract price should be, say, $24 per acre, if it turns out, as that gentleman says, that they are not irrigable, then he claims that they should be got for $8 per acre less. That is the only explanation I can give for the gentleman saying that they would be called upon to pay $8 more in the event of the reclassification upholding the Canadian Pacific railway's contention.
On section 8-use of irrigation works for the storage of water:

The question of administration would arise in applying this section

and I think there should be a full statement as to how it is proposed to exercise the authority which the section will confer on the minister.

As the Act states, the
amendments are for the purpose of preventing any person or company from enjoying a monopoly of the available water supply and more especially if that particular water supply is situated in an advantageous location in reference to ditches. The amendments, while so framed as to protect existing rights, will make provision for the use by others, or by the public, under the direction of the minister, of any works which are not being fully utilized by their owners or which can be advantageously enlarged so as to serve a more useful purpose. There might be certain seasons of the year when there is a drouth and a certain work is not utilized by its owners to its full capacity. OtheT parties desire to use the water and the minister takes power under this provision of utilizing this work for the benefit of persons who have no other opportunity of securing water privileges. To cite an instance: the Alberta Railway and Irrigation Company were requested to allow their works to be utilized in favour of other parties and they were so utilized. I think the proposal explains itself pretty fully. It sets out in detail how the relative costs are to be borne. It states that the minister may fix the amount of compensation to which the owners of the works so utilized are, in his opinion, entitled, and the amount that shall be paid to the owners of such works. The cost of maintaining these works shall be borne as between one applicant and the other and the owners of the works, as they existed before the enlargement, generally in proportion to the quantity of water which each is entitled to use. Where parties have works completed but not utilized to their full capacity it is provided that these works may be utilized on behalf of other parties.

There is a considerable waste of water from the works of the Alberta Railway and Irrigation Company. This water is carried away through the coulees. It has been represented to me that if an arrangement could be made by which this water could be stored it would be of great advantage to farmers and stock-raisers. I might mention the case in which a large quantity of water goes through the Chin coulee which might be stored. If some arrangement could be made with the Government or the irrigation company by which that water could be stored in a reservoir the

people in that particular district would derive a great amount of benefit especially for the watering of stock. At present the water which runs through the Chin coulee is not stored and it does not become of permanent value to the people in that district. The storage of that water would be no loss at all to the irrigation company but it would be of great value to the farmers and settlers there, especially for the watering of stock.

I understand that there is a waste of water down these coulees and I also understand that the company are now making arrangements, by way of the construction of a reservoir, to preserve that water. When the Chin coulee works are completed they will stop the future waste.

This section gives the
minister very extraordinary authority over private property. Is there a precedent for that authority and, if so, where does it exist?

I do not know if there is a precedent but we felt that where works were being taken and utilized by the minister for the general benefit of the public he should have the authority to fix the compensation. I have no precedent in my mind for this authority but in what manner would my hon. friend suggest an alteration in the manner of fixing the compensation?

I did not know but that there was a precedent in some legislation elsewhere, which probably would be an indication as to the way in which the Act could be administered. The reason given for the desirability of this authority I will not question, but I still say it confers a very extraordinary authority upon the minister and I think that in a matter Of providing compensation the minister is possibly taking a measure of responsibility that is not best for his own convenience or in the interest of the individuals concerned. Where the question of compensation comes in I would think there should be provision for arbitration, and in a case where one party materially alters the work of the other party, there is always a possibility of substantial damage being done to the new work, or of the new work being ill-conceived or ill-executed and serious damage suffered by the owner of the original work. There is no provision in the Act to meet such a case. I do not wish to stand in the way of the good administration of the Irrigation Act, but I take this opportunity of calling the attention of the minister to the fact that he is assuming very extraordinary powers here on his individual responsibility, and I think he would be well advised to give the matter more consideration than he evidently has given it up to the present time.

I km informed that there
is a precedent for this in British Columbia, but I am not absolutely certain as to that. It is considered that the minister should take this responsibility, although he is not anxious to insist on any undue responsibility. First of all, the parties have an opportunity o'f coming together and deciding if at all possible as to the amount of the respective cost of the work that should be apportioned by their respective parties, but failing or delaying to agree the minister may fix the amount to be paid by each. It is only when the private users fail to amicably agree on the amount, that the minister is called in as an arbitrator. This Bill has been submitted to quite a number of persons in the West and in the East who are engaged in irrigation, and they thought this was quite essential.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

I wish to amend section 4 of the Act by substituting the following:
Any water, the property of which is vested in the Crown may he acquired for domestic, muncipal, ndust.ial, irrigation, and other purposes including the granting of permission to cstabl sh dams, piers, booms and other necessary works in any non-navigable stream, to facilitate the passage of logs, timber, and other products of the forest along such stream.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I have another amendment to propose. In the original Act Parliament clothes the Minister of the Interior and the Department of the Interior with all the powers and authority as to the expropriation of lands for irrigation purposes which the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Department of Railways and Canals enjoy with regard to the expropriation of lands for railway purposes. Subsequently, however, the Railway Act was amended so as to vest certain powers with respect to expropriation in the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. It has been held by some that the amendment to the Railway Act has curtailed to a certain extent the po,wers of the Minister of the Interior and the Department of the Interior with respect to the expropriation of lands

for irrigation purposes and the object of the amendment I have to propose is to reestablish, if it be necessary, their full authority over such matters without reference to the Board of Railway Commissioners. I am told by legal authorities that it really does not curtail our power but I desire to make it absolutely clear.
Is there any authority now vested in the Board of Railway Commissioners under the Irrigation Act?
Our law department states they have nothing at all to do with the expropriation of lands for irrigation purposes.

Is there any truth in the following despatch from Calgary which appears in the Citizen of this morning?
Calgary, Alta., May 11.-Approximately four hundred thousand acres of land in the southern portion of Alberta will be put under irrigation by the Dominion Government, or by the municipalities which obtain from the Government the right to operate a system of irrigation in the various districts, some time in the near future, according to the statement of F. H. Peters, irrigation commissioner for the Dominion with headquarters in Calgary.

I am informed that the department have made certain surveys north of Lethbridge to determine the character of the land and to see what quantity is available for irrigation; but we have no final report on the subject as yet, and we have not come to any decision regarding the matter. I do not know whether Mr. Peters is referring to that or not. He may be referring to the fact that in the very near future the 400,000 acres of the Canadian Pacific lands will be sufficiently advanced to be thrown open for settlers on the irrigation system. If he refers to the Government land, we have not any final report from the engineer as to the particular character and class of lands and where they are located. I believe they are north of the city where the hon. gentleman resides.

During last summer a survey was made of these lands north of the city of Lethbridge, near the Little Bow.
I do not know exactly the locality of the lands, but I know there was a survey party there; and some of the settlers told me that they were talking to members of this party, and that it was intimated to them that the Government might establish an irrigation system in that particular district so that the farmers could get a supply of water from it under certain arrangements. The settlers are particu-

larly anxious to get this water, especially in the district known as the Iron Springs district. The settlers say that the surveyors were in there examining the possibilities of supplying water to that country, and that the Government had in view the establishment of an irrigation scheme so as to supply the farmers who required it with water for irrigation purposes.
I have not any final report on that.
The question is: Has the Government in contemplation the establishment of a Government irrigation scheme in that particular locality?
The policy of the Government has not been discussed in regard to that matter at all; it has never engaged the attention of the Government.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

I beg to move:
That the following words be added at the end of section 10 :-Nothing in this amending Act shall apply to any case with respect to which litigation is now pending.
-Section as amended agreed to.

stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Judges Act, chapter 138 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, and to provide for the increase of the salaries of three Judges of the Superior Court of Quebec from $5,000 each per annum to $7,000 each per annum and to provide for the salary of an additional Judge of the said Court at $5,000 per annum; to provide for the salaries of three additional puisne Judges of the Supreme Court of Alberta at $6,000 each per annum; to provide for the salary of one junior County Court Judge for the province of Manitoba at $3,000 per annum; to provide for four additional District Court Judges for the province of Saskatchewan at $3,000 each per annum; to provide for the increase of the salary of the senior Judge of the Circuit Court of the district of Montreal from $3,600 to $5,000 per annum, and for the increase of the salaries of the three other Judges of the said Court from $3,000 each per annum to $4,500 each per annum.

Who are the three judges of the Superior Court of the province of

Quebec whose .salaries are to be increased from $5,000 each to $7,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The three judges referred to are the judges who were appointed respectively for the district of Richelieu, Mr. Justice iBiruneau; for the district of St. Hyacinthe, Mr. Justice Martineau; and for the district of Montcalm, Mr. Justice Chauvin.
The judge sits at Mont Laurier, in the district of Montcalm.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the first two judges, the reason of this proposal is that the legislature of the province of Quebec, after consultation between the Prime Minister and Attorney General of the province and myself, as Minister of Justice, has provided that the residences of these two judges should 'be fixed in the city of Montreal, and that they should be expected to devote their entire time outside of their special districts to the service of the district of Montreal. This legislation was enacted after the Attorney General of the province and myself had both agreed that it would be desirable, in the interest of the proper administration of justice, that these two judges should be so transferred to that district. The operation, of course, required the concurrence of both authorities, because, while it is within the power of the legislature of Quebec to define the duties of a judge, and they may by so doing modify the position to which a man has been appointed, it is the function of the Government of Canada to appoint the judge to the position so created. It is to carry out this understanding arrived at that the provision is made with regard to these judges.
I may point out the particular advantage that results. It is undoubted that the services of outside judges, or, failing those services, the appointment of additional judges, are required in the district of Montreal. If this arrangement were not made, it would be quite open to the legislature, in the exercise of its functions, to provide for an additional judge or additional judges for the district of Montreal. If that had been done and two additional judges provided for that district, it would have imposed upon the country a charge of $14,000. Under these arrangements we get the services in Montreal for the bulk of the time of two rural judges tat an additional cost to the country of only $4,000. With regard to the persons who are appointed to
these new positions, this Government is quite prepared, in accordance with the understanding which has been arrived at, to assent to their appointment and recommend the voting of the salaries. With regard to the third gentleman, the situation which has brought about the present position is that under the legislation of the province of Quebec, so long as the court house was not finished at Mont Laurier, the new judge appointed to the district, Judge Chauvin, was to reside in the district of Ottawa. He was -in reality in the position of a second judge in the district of Ottawa. The legislation as originally passed provided that when the court house was completed at Mont Laurier the judge was required to live in that district. That left the district of Ottawa with but one resident judge. It was represented to me and to the Attorney General of the province, that the work in the district of Ottawa required the services of two judges; and certainly, from what knowledge I had on the subject there could be no mistake about that. I was asked whether, if the legislation providing for an additional judge for the district of Ottawa were passed, I would recommend the salary of a judge. I pointed out that as there were a number of judges in the province of Quebec whose districts called for comparatively little work, it would be desirable, instead of adding to the number of judges, that the judge of some other district where the work was not very heavy should be asked to share the work in the district of Ottawa. That view was apparently accepted, both by the Bar of the district of Ottawa who made representations to me and by the Attorney General of the province who in consequence provided that the judge in the district of Montcalm should be a judge for the district of Ottawa, that, in addition to his own work in the district of Montcalm, which is not very heavy, he should give some of his time to sharing the work of the present incumbent of the district of Ottawa. The pro-vinical Government and Legislature considered that the judge serving these two districts, instead of residing in one district and going to the other as occasion might require, could more conveniently reside in the city of Montreal. That is a matter with which this Parliament or Government is not concerned. Under the circumstances, here again is a case where by the combination of work we avoid the appointment

of an additional judge, which, in this case, would have involved $5,000. But as the two districts have been assigned to the one judge, it seemed reasonable that that judge should have .more remuneration than a judge of tout one rural district, and so it is suggested that Judge Chauvm should have $2,000 additional. So by this we economize $3,000, as by the other we economize $10,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As I understand it, three judges are increased from $5,000 to $7,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
One being
Judge Chauvin, the new judge of the district of Montcalm?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And who are the others?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Judge Bruneau of Richelieu and Judge Martineau of St. Hyacinthe.

The Minister of Justice seems to be labouring under the impression that the rural judges can devote some of their time to either Montreal and Quebec, and for this reason two of these judges are assigned to Montreal at an increased salary. The rural judges receive $5,000 and the Montreal judges $7,000. I would like to ask the minister what is the basis of that salary distinction-is it on account of the work or is it on account of the higher cost of living in the larger cities? I may say that if it is on account of the amount of work, the judges in Three Rivers, as I have had occasion to say before, sit every day in the year except vacation, and even then they very often sit, and one has to be in attendance all the time. They have original jurisdiction in a wide range of cases; they hear appeals under municipal and school codes, and they sit as a court of review in the city of Quebec. They do not complain of the work. But I do not see why they should be discriminated against as they certainly are if the salary is based on the. amount of work. If you were to divide the number of cases tried or the judgments rendered at Three Rivers by the number of judges there, and the number of eases tried and judgments rendered in Montreal by the number of judges there, you would find that there is more work done by each of the two judges in Three Rivers than by any individual judge in Montreal. So,
I fail to see why they should not the TMr. Doherty.]
increase. If it is on the basis of the cost of living, then if that matter is investigated it will be found that the cost of living in Three Rivers is just as high in Three Rivers as it is in Montreal, if not higher. Then, as I have pointed out before, the judges in Montreal, being more numerous, have better opportunity to consult together. They have also a very large law library which is kept up by the Bar of the whole province, we may say, because all our students read in Montreal or Quebec and their fees on admission go to these libraries. Our judges have to subscribe for their own reviews, periodicals of jurisprudence and reports. Practically they must have their own library, for our Bar library is not extensive-we are only twenty-two or twenty-three in number in our district. I fail to see why these judges should not have an increase of salary to put them on the same footing as those of Montreal or Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The reasons which led to making a difference between the salaries of judges of the Superior Court sitting in the district of Montreal and Quebec and those sitting in other districts must, of course have been known to those who established that difference. The present scale of salaries was established under a law enacted during the regime of the Government of which the hon. gentleman for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) was the Solicitor General, and I should presume that he would toe in as good a position as any member of this House to indicate the reasons that influenced the Government of that day in making that distinction. For myself, speaking personally, if circumstances were such as to enable me to deal generally with the subject of the salaries of judges, I might be disposed to do more -than is proposed to be done under this legislation. But this legislation accepts the situation, as regards the district of Montreal, which existed when this Government came into power and merely is intended to facilitate the appointment in cases where this Government feels justified in nominating particular judges in rural districts to be judges in a special way of the district of Montreal without being entirely separated from their own districts. We are not modifying the principle upon which the distinction was originally made. As regards judges generally, I might personally be disposed, if circumstances made it possible to do more than is done here. But that would involve dealing with the subject of judges generally,

not only in Quebec, but throughout the Dominion.
I am limiting myself to making provision for additional judges and, with regard to this particular matter, to meeting an arrangement come to on the part of the province and on the part of the Government by which we believe that the administration of justice in the district of Montreal may be improved and, at the same time, an economy effected. I am not in a position to deal with the suggestion that the judges at Three Rivers do more or less work than the judges in the district of Montreal.

The conditions that existed five or six years ago in the district of Three Rivers are vastly different from the conditions that exist there to-day. Since that time the population of the city of Three Rivers has jumped from eleven thousand to eighteen thousand. You know, Mr. Chairman, that the town of Grand Mere, which is in the district of Three Rivers, and which was a wilderness ten years ago, has now a population of 6,000 or 7,000. Industries are constantly springing up and water-powers being developed and no district in the province of Quebec has made such rapid strides forward during the last four or five years as has the district of Three Rivers. The judges in the city of Three Rivers have as much work to do as any judge in Montreal or Quebec. Besides, if it comes down to a question of the cost of living, it costs them as much-if not more -to live in Three Rivers as it costs the judges to live in Montreal or Quebec. The judge, as I have said, has the disadvantage of not having a library at his disposal, and he has to provide one out of his own funds. He has to sit in the Court of Review the same as the judge of any rural district, where the amount df work is not so great. They are sitting every day in the year except during vacation. I do not know why these men, who have to do this large amount of work and with living expenses as great as the living expenses of the judges in Montreal, should not get the same salary as the judges of the Montreal district. I am not talking about the other districts, because I know nothing about them, but I submit that under the circumstances no justifiable reason can be given for the difference between the salaries of the judges in the district of Three Rivers and those in the districts of Montreal and Quebec.

I would like to direct the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that there is a judge residing in the
city of Westmount, near Montreal, who was originally appointed for the district of Pontiac, with residence at Bryson. I understand that the provincial Government has authorized his residence at Westmount in the district of Montreal and asked him to exercise his judicial duties in that district when he is not required in the district of Pontiac. This, it appears to me, places him in very much the same position as the judges of the districts of St. Hyacinthe and Richelieu, whose cases have just been dealt with by the hon. Minister of Justice. This judge would not foe included in this resolution, and I should be very glad if the hon. Minister of Justice would explain why this exception has been made. I believe the judge to whom I refer is Mr. Justice Weir.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I pointed out in dealing with the case of the judges of the Richelieu and St. Hyacinthe districts, the bringing about of a position whereby these two gentlemen enter upon the performance of the duties of the new position created by the legislature of Quebec and will become, if this resolution and the Bill based upon it be passed, entitled to this additional salary, involves action within the jurisdiction of the provincial Government and legislature and action which comes within the functions of the Government and the Parliament of Canada. The reason why the judge originally appointed at Pontiac does not figure in this resolution is that in regard to him there has been neither consultation with this Government nor action by it. The assignment of these _ judges to this new work involves an appointment going beyond the appointment granted by their original commission. It is the function of the Government of Canada to make those appointments; it belongs to the office of the Minister of Justice to make the nominations to those appointments. After looking into the conditions as to the locality of the districts of the two judges of Richelieu an'd St. Hyacinthe, from the point of view of proximity to Montreal, and after consideration of the qualifications of these gentlemen, I have come to the conclusion that I was perfectly justified in nominating them for these positions of wider usefulness and greater responsibility. Being ready to do that, and my nomination being acceptable to the Government of Canada, which must take the responsibility; we are proceeding accordingly. Not having been consulted at all about the arrangement which the legislature of the province of Quebec thought proper to

make with regard to the district of Pontiac, I was not, of course, called upon before it was ma>de either to form or to express any opinion. After its having been made, it is quite true that it might be possible, if I as Minister of Justice were prepared to take the responsibility of the nomination and this Government were prepared to take the responsibility of the appointment, that we might appoint the gentleman who fills the position under his commission of judge of the district of Pontiac to this new sphere of action. Without going into any discussion that would in any way be derogatory to the gentleman concerned, after full consideration of the circumstances-in the first place, that the district of Pontiac is very remote from the district of Montreal and, in ' the second place, that there are a number of judges in rural (districts much nearer to Montreal who could much more conveniently have been called to the performance of these duties-and after [DOT] considering also the question of whether in my judgment, and upon my responsibility I ought to nominate this particular gentleman for the position, I have not been disposed to take the responsibility of making that nomination.
Are these three judges whose salaries are increased from $5,000 to $7,000 at present residing in the city of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether Mr. Justice Bruneau and Mr. Justice Mar-tineau have changed their residences since this enactment of the Quebec Legislature, nor am I quite certain where they were actually residing before the change. I would assume that they were residing at St. Hyaointhe and at Sorel.
Then in addition to receiving $7,000, every day they sit in Montreal they will claim ten dollars a day for living expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The law already prevents that.
Where will the new judges for the Superior Court in Quebec reside?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are to be two
judges in the district of Saguenay. My impression is that the one thus added is to live at Chicoutimi.

What is the present necessity for this legislation? I understood a couple of months ago that there would be 
a revision of the salaries of judges all along the line. Now we find two or three judicial positions in Quebec singled out for special consideration. Have the judges in Quebec struck for more pay? There are judges in the other provinces doing their duty quite as well as those in Quebec, and if consideration is to be given to those in one province why should it not be given to those in the others? It seems to me that the minister is making an invidious distinction in favour of these judges in Quebec. The Supreme Court judges in Alberta are to receive $6,000 but these strikers are to receive $7,000. I want to know why these judges in Quebec are receiving this special consideration while those in other provinces are receiving no consideration at all. I think the salaries of judges, taken on the whole, are just about as large as they should be. I am a member of the profession-and I know something of what I am talking about. The salaries received by judges of the various courts throughout Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, are in about ninety per cent of the .cases considerably in excess of the amount the judges made at the Bar. Laymen are asking where this is going to stop and why these men, who are retiring usually into positions of comparative ease and munificence of the Government, receive salaries much greater than their former incomes, although they do much less work. Very good reasons should be given for an increase of $2,000 per annum in a judge's salary. Unfortunately, I was not present when the minister began his explanation of this resolution, but I would like to hear reasons strong enough to convince me that this is legislation for which I should vote.
At six o clock, the Committee took recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was about to say
when the House rose at six o'clock that if the hon. gentleman who spoke last had been present when I made my explanation he would have perceived that this is not a question of making an increase in the judges' salaries or of making any discrimination in favour of any province. This legislation is the result of an endeavour to improve the system, and by means of that improvement in the system to arrive at an improvement in the administration of justice in the district of Montreal in a way more economical than it otherwise could be arrived at. The great centre of legal

business in the province of Quebec is the district of Montreal. The population of that district must be in the neighbourhood of 800,000 people, and the judges are in large numbers scattered through the rural districts. If we proceeded in the ordinary way, what would happen would be that the legislature of the province of Quebec would ibe entitled, if the business of the Montreal district required it, to provide for two additional judges in the district of Montreal, and that would have made two additional salaries for the Dominion to pay. There being need for further aid, and there being men available the duties of whose districts do not take up all of their time, under this arrangement we aTe getting a transfer into the place where the work is to be done of two men at an additional cost of $4,000, instead of $14,000. Instead of the province of Quebec providing for two new judges and two full salaries, we are utilizing the services of men who are entitled to a salary of $5,000 a year at a cost to the Dominion of $4,000. After this explanation there can be no question of discrimination, and I feel sure that my hon. friend's terror of strikers will disappear.
Will Mr. Justice Chauvin do work in the district of Montreal also?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As far as it may be possible, but I believe he will have enough to do in the district of Ottawa and in his own district of Montcalm. I do not anticipate then that he will have very much time after he has done his work in the district of Ottawa. If an arrangement had been made for a resident judge in the district of Ottawa there would have been also a judge in Mont Eaurier, and it would have been necessary to provide a salary for an aduitional judge, which would have meant an extra expense of $5,000 a year. Acting upon the suggestion I made, which was concurred in by the provincial authorities, instead of doing that arrangements have been made by the provincial authorities to have this judge take, in addition to the work of his own district, his share of the work in the Ottawa district. Again, instead of an additional judge with salary of $5,000 a year, we get an additional judge doing the same work at an extra cost of only $2,000. The whole thing has given me a good deal of thought. 1 was rather disposed to congratulate myself an having brought about a most economical arrangement, and I did not expect to be criticised as adding unduly to the expenses in this province.

Has the minister been
