able to make an arrangement with regard to the judicial work in Terrebonne, Joliette and Beauharnois?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In regard to the district of Terrebonne, there has been such an arrangement for a great many years. The judge of Terrebonne resides and works in the district of Montreal. Last year we made a similar arrangement in regard to the district of Beauharnois.
How many Superior Court judges are there in Quebec, and how many Supreme Court judges?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The total number of the Superior Court judges is forty-one. There are no judges under the name of Supreme Court judges. The Superior Court in Quebec is a court that has entire jurisdiction in first instance save in regard to cases under $100. From $100 up the Superior Court has entire jurisdiction in all civil litigation in first instance.

This matter has been coming up from time to time since it was settled some years ago, as appears by the Revised Statutes of 1906. Amendments have been made from time to time, and a few years ago the principle adopted was that judges should be appointed according to population. I suppose the amount of litigation among >a given number of people is about the same all over Canada. The number of judges would be 'about the same in different provinces in proportion to population. I think that there is just as much litigation in the eastern part of Canada as there is in the middle part, in Quebec, in Ontario, or in the West. But we find that there is a discrimination. We find that the chief justice of Prince Edward Island gets only as much as a puisne judge in Manitoba or in Quebec and that puisne judges in Prince Edward Island only get $5,000 a year. I do not think this is right. If we have about the same population to a judge as Quebec has, why should the judges in eastern Canada be discriminated against in this way? The judges in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick do just as much work as the majority of the judges in Quebec, Ontario or Alberta, but we find on the statute books a discrimination in favour of every one of these provinces as against the smallest province in Canada. I brought this question to the attention of the former Minister of Justice

some years ago and I also brought it to the attention of the present Minister of Justice but I was told that there was no change being made in the Act contained in the Revised Statutes of 1906. I cannot see it in that way. I find that there is a change made in judges salaries in this very resolution. The resolution reads in this way:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Judges Act, chapter 13S of the Revised Statutes, 1906, and to provide for the increase of the salaries of three judges of the Superior Court of Quebec from $5,000 each per annum to $7,000 each per annum and to provide for the salary for an additional judge of the said court at $5,000 per annum.
I would like to know how it is that these three judges are to get am additional $2,000 and that the new judge who is to be appointed will only receive $5,000 a year, the same as the puisne judges in Prince Edward Island. I suppose that probably next year another Bill will come in to give this puisne judge an additional $2,000 a year because there will be a lot of kicking over this matter on account of this discrimination. If you look up the statutes you will find that all the other puisne judges receive $6,000. This law in regard to judges should be put upon a proper basis. There should be no discrimination and they should receive equal salaries in all parts of Canada. Important cases come up in the smaller provinces as in the larger provinces, and the same care and attention have to he given them by the judge. In New Brunswick they have only one judge for fifty thousand inhabitants, while in Alberta and Saskatchewan they have one judge for thirty thousand inhabitants, so that these new provinces have been favoured in that way, and the judges receive large salaries as well. The reason given for these larger salaries is on account of the high cost of living, but I think you will find that the cost , of living is about equal in every part of Canada. There may be a difference for the man who wants to live high, but so far as the ordinary cost of living is concerned, not the cost of high living, it is about the same all over. There should be no discrimination and no favouritism shown in the salaries of public officials in this country who do their duty. I think you will find that the judges in eastern Canada do their duty as well and are just as competent as the judges in Quebec, Ontario, the middle west or British Columbia. I ask the Minister of Justice to withdraw this resolution and reconsider it, and I have no doubt this House will do
[Mr. A. A. McLean
justice to the judges from one end of the country to the other if a proper resolution is placed before it.

I have had occasion to discuss this subject many times during the last six or seven years in this House, and I want to say to the Minister of Justice tonight what I have said to my own political friends when they were in power. I heartily concur in everything which has been said by my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. A. A. McLean). I am sure the Minister of Justice does not appreciate the position of the county court judges in the Maritime provinces. They occupy a different position altogether from the county court judges in the rest of Canada. I do not know exactly what the status of the Circuit court judges in Montreal is, but I assume they occupy somewhat the same position as do county court judges in the Maritime provinces. In the Maritime provinces we have only two classes of judges: Superior Court judges and county court judges. I appreciate that the minister meets with a great deal of difficulty in increasing the salary of the county court judges in the Maritime provinces, because of the rather peculiar anomaly which exists in the province of Ontario, where there are two judges for practically every county, and I suppose the minister feels that, as these judges have not very much to do, it would not be reasonable to increase their salaries to, say, $5,000 per annum. But the minister should remember that, in the Maritime provinces, instead of having two judges in a county, each judge has from three to five counties to attend to, and in the western portion of New Brunswick the judge of the county court has four counties under his jurisdiction.
The hon. gentleman is not quite correct when he says that in the province of Ontario almost each county has two judges. That is not the case.
There may be instances to which my remark would not apply, but there must be a great many counties in Ontario where there are two judges.
There are quite a number, but there are more which have only one judge.

Well, that makes no difference to my argument, because I say that in the Maritime provinces each county judge takes from three to five

counties, and is an important official. Besides attending to the holding of courts, he has to take speedy triads, and that necessitates travel over very great distances. I think the minister should take these things into consideration, and realize that, if there are different conditions in any part of the country, these conditions should be specially provided for. I know that the Minister of Justice has been importuned, the same as have other ministers of justice, in regard to this matter, but, notwithstanding what my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) says, if the minister would take the House into his confidence I think he would have to admit that his difficulty in doing justice to the Maritime province judges is because of the peculiar conditions existing in Ontario. If however the Minister of Justice can depart from the general rule and provide increased salaries for judges in Montreal and elsewhere in the province of Quebec, surely he can find means to give a reasonable salary to the judges in the Maritime provinces. It is unnecessary to argue the matter farther; I have called the attention of the Minister of Justice to it on at least two occasions since he became minister, and I do hope that before the Bill passes he will see his way clear to in some way arrange matters so that these important officials in our part of Canada shall receive a reasonable allowance for their services.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	Considering the large
number of judges in the province of Quebec, the advance is a small one, but no doubt it will be gratifying to the recipients of it. It is, however, a step in the right direction. I do not pretend to understand the divisions of the judiciary in the province of Quebec, but it appears from the Judges' Act that there are at least three classes of judges: the judges of the Superior Court, of which there are quite a number, the district judges, who do not preside in the Superior Courts and who evidently would correspond to County Court judges in the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the province of Quebec, what the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) describes as district judges are judges of the Superior Court, but each has assigned to him <a particular district. Some of these Superior Court judges are assigned to the district of Montreal, some to the district of Quebec, and the others to rural districts. We have no County Court judges in the province of Quebec. All are Superior
Court judges with the exception of four Circuit Court judges in the city and district of Montreal. All of the judges who sit in the first instance are judges of the Superior Court, but although there is a difference in the salary paid that difference is based presumably upon the fact that in the large districts of Montreal and Quebec the work is vastly heavier than in the' rural districts.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	The Supreme Court
judges in Nova Scotia are supposed to live in the capital city of Halifax and they go on circuit and act as a court of appeal sitting en banc. There is a court of appeal in the province of Quebec which I presume is composed of some of the Superior Court judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The court of appeal in Quebec is a separate court called the Court of King's Bench.
Mr. MeKENZIE: That is, as I understand it, that they do not go on circuit. Those judges, whose jurisdiction is confined to districts, are doing what is really County Court work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They do both Superior Court work and county court work.
Mr. MeKENZIE: The same thing is true absolutely of the county court judges in the province of Nova Scotia. The hon. minister knows that with very few exceptions a county court judge can try every kind of crime with the consent of the accused. Murder, or attempt to murder and a very few other cases cannot be tried without a jury. In the province of Nova Scotia a county court judge is a Master in Chambers of the Supreme Court. As such, almost every kind of work comes before him. As we have only one set of Supreme Court judges and that set residing in Halifax, it is very easily understood that everything that can bo done by our different Bars throughout the province of Nova Scotia before the local masters is done. For instance, in the county of Cape Breton we have a local Bar and a great deal of legal work is done. No lawyer goes to Halifax except to attend the Appeal Court; and consequently the county court judge is sitting every day, trying the cases in his regular courts, sitting as a Master in Chambers or sitting as a Criminal Court, trying criminals, so that every day in the year our county court judge is engaged in some kind of business in connection with the discharge of his duties. A salary of $3,000 a year for a man occupying a position of that

character, and requiring as a judge to have such a wide knowledge of the profession to which he belomw. is not sufficient pay. While it may be difficult to change the situation which has lasted for a great many years, it may he a good opportunity for the minister to deal with the matter at the present time. I was rather sorry to hear the comments made from the other sifde of the House that judges were being paid ample salaries at present. The fact must not be lost sight of that a judge is not in the same position as the ordinary man getting a salary, because there is a certain standing that a judge must maintain; there is a certain dignity of his calling that he must observe, and there is further a provision in the Judges' Act that he must not do other work. There was a time when he could take an interest in companies as a director or as a trustee, and could earn some money in that way; but under the present Judges' Act, passed in the year 1905, he is excluded from all such things, and is not permitted to do anything whatever except that which appertains to his calling as a judge. Therefore he has no income of any kind except his salary. Unfortunately we have only human beings and human nature to contend with in judges just as in men in other positions, and it is well and proper that the man who has to administer the laws should be absolutely independent of any temptation that poverty brings. We fortunately throughout Canada have no complaint to make in regard to the character of our judges, and it is well that we should maintain the dignity of the Bench as far as possible.
As far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, I suppose the hon. minister would have no complaint to make if we had a county court judge for each county in the province. In the province of Ontario there is an average of more than one judge for every county, whereas in the province of Nova Scotia we have eighteen counties and only seven judges. Supposing that in the beginning we had a judge for each county, that would be eighteen judges; and as they would certainly be paid $3,000 a piece, that would be $54,000. With the small number of jufdges that we have, if you give them each $5,000 a piece, it is only $35,000, as compared with $54,000. Seeing that we have cut down the number of judges to seven, I think we have a right to expect that they shall be decently paid, and $5,000 is certainly not asking too much.
In the province of Ontario, county court

judges earn something as surrogate judges; that is they discharge some functions as judges of probate, for which they are paid fees, and it makes a considerable addition to their income. They have also something to do with the assessment lists; they sit at a court of revision or appeal, and for this work they are paid something. In the province of Nova Scotia, however, the county court judge by way of his office is the court of appeal from the decisions of the probate court, but he gets no allowance for that work at all; he gets the bare amount of his salary. I mention this so that the minister will know that there is no analogy between the position of a county court judge of the province of Nova Scotia and that of a county court judge of the province of Ontario, so far as that is concerned.
I think the minister had a different idea in his mind some time ago, namely that he could deal in a general way with this matter, and assist the judges throughout the whole of Canada, particularly in the Maritime provinces. I am sorry to find that the prospects are not so bright as they were eighteen months or two years ago. I hope that the idea put forward by my hon. friend for Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. A. A. McLean), will be followed out and that this resolution will be withdrawn and a wider one submitted. We all understand that it is not competent for the minister to amend the resolution now before the committee, but it certainly would be competent for him to withdraw it and submit one dealing more generally with this question.
There is another matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, as I did on a former occasion. I explained to the minister on that occasion that the county court judge for my district had been deprived of his allowance for travelling expenses under a regulation which assumes to discriminate between different classes of work performed by county court judges. It seems to me a poor matter that, when a county court judge is carrying out the demands of the legislature of the province he should be paid less than the regular travelling allowance. Section 18 of the Judges Act does not recognize any such discrimination. It is as follows:
There shall be paid for travelling allowances to each judge, whether of a Superior or county court, and to each local judge in Admiralty of the Exchequer Court, except as in this section otherwise provided, in addition to his moving or transportation expenses, the sum of six dollars for each day, including necessary days of travel going and returning, during which he is attending as such judge in court or

chambers at any place other than that at which he Is by law obliged to reside.
That is a broad provision that when a judge of the county court is sitting as a court-as he was in the case I have in mind-acting under the provisions of the statutes of the province of Nova Scotia, he certainly comes within the provision of that section. I was certainly surprised that under that regulation the judge was deprived of his proper fees. As I said, I brought this matter to the attention of the minister before. But he has many matters to attend to, and, I quite understand, tends to lose sight of small matters of this hind. But I remind him of it again in the hope that the regulation will be removed, and that when a judge of the county court travels in the regular discharge of his duty, he shall be given, without hesitation and without trouble, the fees allowed under the Act.
However, that is a matter of detail. I would again urge upon the minister the necessity of dealing liberally with the county court judges in the province of Nova Scotia, in the Maritime provinces generally, and indeed all over Canada.
. Mr. McCUBDY: Not having the pleasure and advantage of 'belonging to the legal profession, I cannot appreciate to the same extent as the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) the demands which are made on the time of a county court judge. It is quite evident that the demands made upon him call upon him to be self-sacrificing, and it becomes ingrained in has nature, for has not the hon. member himseif relinquished a position at $3,000 a year as county court judge to accept a much smaller honorarium in the service of his country? But, seriously, it seems to me- and I have made representations to the minister upon the subject at different times -that the remuneration given to our county court judges is quite inadequate. It has remained the same for many years, although, as hon. members are so often reminded, the cost of living has been increasing. There is no way, as the hon. member for North Cape Breton has pointed out, whereby the man who occupies the position of county court judge can increase his income, he is dependent on the salary attached to his position. He is expected to keep up a certain style of living and it seems to me that taking into consideration the constantly increasing expenditure, this is a matter which might well claim the minister's attention. Some of the districts
in Nova Scotia cover quite a wide area. One which I have particularly in mind covers three counties. I would like to add my word to that of others in support of consideration being given particularly to an increase in the salaries of the county court judges.

Why has the Minister of Justice left out the Superior Court judges of Montreal? I find there is no hope for them under the present ruling, though no man knows better than the hon. minister himself the amount of work these judges have to do. I think each of them does as much work as almost any two judges outside of the city. The judges all over the country ought to be well paid, there is no question about that. There is no use of this Government saying that they cannot afford it or that they decline to do it on the ground of economy. A government that has the reputation of burning the candle at both ends must not save on poor judges.

Our judges of both District and Supreme Courts are very inadequately paid. I believe that there are very few judges in Canada to-day who could not make double their salaries in the practice of their profession. The judges that I know anything about in the province of Nova Scotia and one or two of the other provinces, are men who were of the very highest standing at the Bar in their respective provinces, and who, had they remained in practice would be making salaries of from $18,000 to $25,000 a year instead of the $6,000 or $7,000. which they now receive. If there is one class of our public servants -and 1 suppose judges are to a greater or lesser extent public servants-who are very meagerly paid, that class is our judges both of the county and Supreme courts. The judges of the county court in our province and I suppose the same is true in other provinces-receives only $3,000 a year. Any man, if he has sufficient ability to be appointed county court judge, could make double that money in the practice of his profession. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) has referred to my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) having resigned his county court judgeship. If the hon. member for North Cape Breton had given the same attention to his profession that he did to the duties of his position as county court judge, he would have made $4,000 to $8,000 a year instead of the $3,000 he was paid-and

probably that had something to do with his giving up the job.
My remark was entirely commendatory of the action of the hon. member.

I know. Especially in
the district of Cape Breton island, our county court judge does an amount of work that is worthy of double the salary that is paid him.
I need not repeat what 'has been said by the hon. member for North Cape Breton, but our county court judge is busy from Monday morning at nine o'clock until Saturday afternoon at three. He tries practically all criminal cases, with the exception of those of a more serious character; he assumes the duties of master of the Supreme Court at chambers; he hears all interlocutory applications that are made in the various stages of cases sent up to the Supreme Court for trial-my hon. friend the minister of Justice will know what that means in a district where there is a considerable amount of litigation. He is the taxing master and he has the jurisdiction to try civil cases of a very important nature. I mention his case not because I hold a brief for him, but because I know something of his duties, and I believe that he does more work than any other county court judge in the province, excepting, perhaps the judge at Halifax. I cannot understand why this or any other Government should pay a man in that position only |3,000 a year, an absolutely inadequate sum. Many of our tradesmen and smaller merchants, who have not had to go to the expense of acquiring technical knowledge, make more money than that in a year. The judges are absolutely unable to live up to the standard demanded by the dignity of their office on the salaries which they receive.
They can resign.

If it were not for the fact that I would probably be dealing in personalities, I could point out to my hon. friend very many cases where judges have resigned and taken up the practice of their profession simply because they could in that way earn double the amount which they received as judges.
What about the hon. Minister of Justice ?

I believe that if the hon. Minister of Justice would devote to the practice of his profession the careful attention which he gave to his duties as judge

of the Supreme Court, he would make double the amount of money which he received as a judge. But we have to have judges, and in my humble opinion the minister is going to have some difficulty in getting the very best men to act as judges of the Supreme Court if the salaries are to be left as they are at present.
Does the hon. gentleman really think that in this the twentieth century the whole trend of civilization and culture has been such that now everything is measured in dollars and cents?

The hon. gentleman is ahead of his time; he is living in the twenty-eight, not in the twentieth century. He is one of those men who can see the commerce of this country being carried on by flying machines; he is living in the twenty-fourth century at least. But, no matter in what century we are living, to my mind the question is: are the judges of our courts to be paid adequate salaries? The hon. Minister of Justice is taking a forward step in this matter, but I do not think he is taking a step that will commend itself to the country at large. It is all very well to increase the salaries of some particular judges from $5,000 to $7,000 and from $3,000 to $5,000, but I think the Minister of Justice and his department should go thoroughly into the whole question and come to the conclusion that an increase should be given to every judge in Canada, whether he be j udge of the smaller or of the Superior and Supreme Courts. If the minister will see fit to bring down legislation to that end, I believe it would have the hearty support of every gentleman in this House.

I desire to congratulate the minister upon his attempt to make a forward step along the lines of economy in dealing with the question of the judges of our courts. As I understand the idea of the minister, he is going to enlarge the territorial jurisdiction of the county court judges and let them do work in adjoining or neighbouring counties. In that way, by a slight increase in their salaries, he will obviate the necessity of the appointment of a higher salaried judge in the county to which the judge in question is sent. I think that is commendable and should meet with the approval of this House, especially in an age when it is sometimes considered proper to attack men who sit on the Bench of the country. I pay tribute to the thoughtfulness of the minister in providing a little more work and a little more pay for some

of the county court judges. My own idea, being fairly well acquainted with the conditions in Ontario, is that there is gross inequality of pay, having Tegard to the labour performed. Leaving out altogether the rather unique and sensible idea to which the hon. member for West Peterborough has given utterance, I claim that many judges throughout the province of Ontario are doing three times as much work as they are paid for doing. There are a great many judges in Ontario who do not earn the money they are getting; yet no one could ask them to take less, because they have always to be on duty and to perform the services from day to day which a judicial officer must perform. In the county that I have the honour to represent the judge of the county court is a very estimable gentleman, formerly a member of this House, who is held in the highest esteem by the litigating public. He is a very busy man, as the county is a great litigating county; we call it the fighting county. I am quite certain that I could pick out throughout the province of Ontario six county court judges who together do less work than the judge of the county court in the county of Perth. That being the case, the principle that the minister is endeavouring to establish by this Bill might be fairly established to-day in respect of the county court judges in the province of Ontario. While I admit that as the province of Ontario is growing rapidly in industrial life, the work of the judges will increase very rapidly and the day may come when these men of whom I speak may have more than enough to do, still I believe that it would be worth the minister's while extending the principle not only to Quebec but to the province of Ontario as well.
And to Nova Scotia.

I cannot speak of the conditions in Nova Scotia, but I heard the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) eloquently speaking for the Superior Court judges a moment ago. So far as Ontario is concerned, I have heard no complaint about their salaries, but there is complaint at times from the public that while this Parliament has enacted a law which compels the retirement of county court judges at seventy-five years, it is entirely left open so that a judge of the Superior Court may stay on the bench until he is 175 years old, if he lives that long. I do (not think the discrimination is a fair one. I believe that the county court judge throughout Ontario and within the whole Dominion jurisdiction is in every 228
respect as estimable a man and as worthy of the consideration of Governments as any Supreme Court or Superior Court judge, and I, for one, feel that since the law has been applied, and I think in many eases well applied, that a judge having reached the age of 75 is forced to retire from the county court judgeship, his brother on the Superior Court bench, who has enjoyed more than double the salary all his life, sho'uld be put in the same position. While I will have to make exceptions, owing to the fact of men of 75, such as Chancellor Boyd in Ontario, retaining all their faculties in splendid shape so that they are able apparently to do their work as well as at any time, so that it would be a distinct loss to the bench if they were forcibly retired; there are to-day in Ontario some complaints at the non-retirement of Superior Court judges who have reached the age at which a county court judge would be forcibly retired. I congratulate the minister on his advance towards economy on this line and the application of the sensible plan of giving the county court judges a little more work and adding to their pay.

I cannot say that I agree altogether with the remarks of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy). It seems to me that the question of economy should not arise in connection with the salaries of judges. If the Government are going to practise economy, cutting down or keeping low, the salaries of judges would seem to me to be a very poor place to begin it. It would be better for the Government to begin in the Militia Department an'd cut down the construction of drill-halls, or perhaps in the Public Works Department, where the expenditure has been going up by leaps and bounds in the last three or four years.
There seems to be a general agreement between members on both sides that the salaries of district or county court judges in Saskatchewan should be somewhat increased. If that is true in Nova Scotia or in parts Oif Ontario or in Quebec, it is equally true in the western parts of Canada and particularly so in Saskatchewan, not only on account of the fact that the judges in that province are all working from morning until night, as there are not sufficient County Court judges in the province, but also because living is much more expensive in that part of the country than in any other part of Canada. In an ordin-



ary county town, in Ontario a man occupying the position of county court judge can live on much less than he could in a similar town in Saskatchewan. I attended a banquet given by the Bar Association of Saskatchewan to the Minister of Justice last fall. The minister was in particularly good humour on that occasion after he had been banqueted and treated to the best that the prairies produce. I understood from his remarks, and the impression was general not only in Regina but in Moosejaw, that he was going to do something
9	p.m. to increase the salaries of county court judges in Saskatchewan. I know that the minister's answer will be that he must deal with the whole of Canada; but the conditions are somewhat different in the West as it costs more to live and the judges there actually do more work than county court judges in Ontario. I hope the minister will devise some scheme by which he can be of some assistance to the judges of the county court in Saskatchewan. The minister is going to appoint four more District Court judges in that province. He will have trouble in getting proper men for those positions at $3,000. He shakes his head. I venture to say that a great many of the applications he has had for the position are from men not fitted to occupy the position of county court judge. I know that he cannot get properly qualified men for these positions at a salary of $3,000. Unless the salaries are made adequate to the position the minister will not be able to get the best men to occupy the positions of District Court judges in the western provinces, and I hope that some means will be found to give these men more salary than they are offered at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, before
this resolution is put, I wish to once more state my views as to its purport. The hon. minister stated that the Judges-' Act should be amended. I must say, in the first place, that I am greatly pleased at the rapid spread of the views I expounded in the course of this session concerning the proposed increase in the Judges' salaries. Despite the lateness of the season, the seed which I have put in the soil is making good progress, if I am to judge by the statements forthcoming from the hon. member (Mr. Fowler) before recess, and I have reason to believe that before long it- will yield a magnificent crop.

I have several times addressed the House in this connection, and I must -say once more that I cannot agree with the views expressed by my hon, friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll); and neither can I agree with -the views expressed by another of my colleagues, who has just taken his seat (Mr. Martin of Regina) when he stated, as the previous gentleman had also stated, that the judges- were being paid starvation wages. Starvation wages, you say, with $7,000 for the Superior court judges and $3,000 for the County court judges of Ontario and the other provinces?
If such be the case, I wonder how many people we will lose in this country within a year or two, when those who are drawing such salaries aTe bound to disappear from the face of the earth on account of the increased cost of living. I wonder how many people there will be left in the country following on such a disaster. Is it not a fact that we have, in this country, a large number of people, earning less than, five-, six, seven hundred dollars, one thousand or twelve hundred dollars, while burdened with families to bring up and children to educate? However, not a single lawyer in this House has as yet risen from his seat to urge on the Government the desirability of increasing the wages of these people who are threatened with starvation. Not a single legal gentleman on either side of the House has done. so.
That question of the judges' salaries is entirely a novel one for the electorate, and I say that the people are ignorant of what is going on in this connection. But the people will -be informed of the facts, and I for one, have quite made up my mind to take up the subject whenever an occasion offers.
Most lawyers are willing to accept these judgeships at $7,000 or $8,000 per annum, realizing that in so doing, they are providing for their old age a pension, after fifteen or twenty years' service, without ever contributing to the fund. Is there in any part of the country people who draw superannuation without beforehand contributing to the fund off the-ir salary cheque? Only the judges enjoy that privilege.
As stated by my hon. friend from Queens and Albert, at the time of recess, many legal gentlemen who are promoted to the Bench never, while practising at the Bar, had the chance of drawing a monthly cheque of between $416 and $580, such as they receive from the Government. Far from it, I may say that to my knowledge, many lawyers who were eking out a mere living in Montreal, or elsewhere, were most happy to ac-

cept positions in the Civil Service, because they [DOT]could not make both ends meet out of their professional fees; and now we are told that the judges should be paid larger salaries. I say that is preposterous.
What example are you professional men setting for the people? I say that in taking such a stand you are abetting the other classes of .society against you; you are making yourself an object of envy to them, because you are keeping everything for yourselves and leaving nothing for others'. But the time is near when a stop will have to be put to it.
I have already spoken to the same effect on several occasions, but I wish to-day to make an exception in favour of the judges of the Montreal Circuit Court. I am in favour of increasing the salaries of those judges, the senior of whom has heretofore drawn only $3,600 per annum, while his colleagues drew $3,000. I say that those judges are not sufficiently paid for the work they are doing, and1 besides they have no right to a pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: After twenty-five years.

Well, that is wrong. I
am against granting any pension to them. If both parties in this House are agreed as to the desirability of paying larger salaries to the judges, why not pay them while they are doing the work? There is no reason for that pension. It is . to that the people object.
Why is that pension granted to the Superior Court judges, instead of a larger salary? Why? Simply in order to enable the party in power to appoint as judges those who are unwilling to face public opinion, and that, by pensioning the retiring judges, so as to make room for others. The hon. Minister of Justice is posted in this connection. Possibly he will deny it, but 1 challenge him to come and discuss, that question on the hustings in the province of Quebec, and I am satisfied that he will not defend before the people the stand he is now taking.
The hon. Minister of Justice, stated that, by means of this resolution, he expected to effect a saving of $12,000 per annum by getting those three judges to sit in Montreal. The minister has thus adopted the right course; I may congratulate him right here, for those $12,000 will put us in a position to continue paying that pension to him for some time to come. But that pension will have to be dispensed with some day, and I beg of him to speak in my behalf to the right hon. Prime Minister, so that the 2281
House may be afforded an opportunity of discussing the Bill which I introduced at the opening of the session. The Government should not entertain any fears since they have the majority in this House.
I am not speaking for myself alone. True, I am not a lawyer, but what I say is in the interest of those poor people who work hard and strain every nerve to earn a few hundred dollars, and I am. waging war on the magnates who would gobble everything and leave nothing to others.
I see that the few hon. gentlemen who have taken part in this debate belong to the legal profession. I think they expect to be promoted to the Bench one of these days. Among them, there are some men of mature years, and others much younger. For instance, my hon. friend from Sourh Cape Breton is young; he is a good lawyer and he will be made a judge before long. My hon. friend from Queens, P.E.I., is anxious that the judges' salaries should be increased; I surmise that he will be made a judge pretty soon; his stand on the question would seem to indicate it. I must say in conclusion that I am strongly opposed tc any increase of the salaries of suen judges as are drawing just now $8,000, $7,000, or even $5,000, and I say that the country is at one with me on that point.

I was very much disappointed with the fact that the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) had not succeeded in dealing with this question of the judges' salaries in a comprehensive way, as he assured us last year he would do in the interval. I cannot follow my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) in the congratulations which he has given to the minister wherein he says that some economy has been practised as a result of this resolution. I have always been under the impression that the constitution of the courts, the statement as to the number of judges that should exist, and all the provisions in that particular, rest entirely in the hands of the provincial legislatures, and all that is necessary for the Minister of Justice to do is to provide for the appointment of judges and fix their salaries. The minister, in dealing with this case, has devoted his energy entirely to one province of the Dominion. I need not repeat the arguments that have been made by the two hon. members from Cape Breton as to the necessity for a prompt ana early consideration of the conditions which exist in the province from which i come; but I apprehend that in other prov-

inces of the Dominion the question is quite as acute as it is in the province of Quebec or in the province of Nova Scotia. I think that the gentlemen who are on the bench were led to believe last year by the minister that this whole question of the revision of salaries would- have been considered between sessions and would have been dealt with this year. I have not heard any explanation from my hon. friend the minister as to why, in (dealing with this question, he has limited his efforts to one province. One does not need to repeat the arguments which have been made on behalf of the Opposition. On the other hand, we have had some suggestions as to the lack of any necessity for moving, but I am sure that the practice which has always characterized the payment of the judiciary in the empire, the custom that has been set for us in the Parliament of the mother country, where salaries which would almost be regarded here as princely accompany the filling of the judicial office, has marked a condition of affairs which I think might well be continued in this country. When we recall the fact that the life, the liberty and possibly everything there is in the world belonging to the individual may be destroyed or completely nullified as the result of the decisions of the men who have been appointed by the state to sit in judgment in regard to the particular issues involved, we will at once realize that we have a condition in which nothing but the most unswerving integrity and the highest degree of independence should characterize the occupant of the bench who has these questions to determine. Anything that would detract from that superb independence which is absolutely essential to the proper administration of the law and the maintenance of those high standards of legal jurisprudence on which the very best interests of our country depend would be the greatest possible menace to the state. These considerations which, I have no doubt, have been put by hon. gentlemen who have spoken before me, must have appealed to the minister, and I only desire to again express my regret that in dealing with this question he has only touched the fringe of it and not attempted to deal with it on those broad lines which we anticipated last year he would have done.

I want to point out to the minister that we are finding fault with the increases granted to certain judges in
[ Mr. Macdonald. ]
Quebec who, while it is true they are not county court judges, yet, from the information which we all have, we know are practically performing the same service as county court judges in the other provinces. I do not think the minister should go behind any such technicality as that. He may claim that there are particular circuit judges who are doing a large amount of work, but I venture the assertion that they are doing no greater amount of work than many of the county court judges are in the Maritime provinces. Take the county court judge of Sydney, the county court judge of Halifax, the county court judge of St. John, or the county court judges of many of the rural districts and compare the amount of work they do with the work that these judges do in Quebec, and the comparison, I venture to say, will be very favourable to the county court judges of the Maritime provinces. You have also to take into consideration the fact that in the Maritime provinces there are often three and four counties joined together in one circuit. I am afraid the minister does not appreciate the condition of affairs. The statement was made by one hon. member this evening that large demands were made upon their time. It is not so much the demands that are made upon the time of the county court judges, but it is the fact that, owing to the high position they occupy, they cannot do anything else and they are simply compelled to live upon their $3,000 a year or resign their position. They are prohibited from taking part in any other of the activities of life. The county court judge occupies, so to speak, just as high a position as the Lord 'Chief Justice of England does; that is, he is not in a position to engage in business, he cannot increase his salary by any outside transactions, he cannot even be a director in a joint stock company, and he has to live up to a standard just the same as a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or the Lord Chief Justice of England. My hon. friend may say that they have no difficulty in getting men to take these positions. That may be true, but my hon. friend will find that he has a lot of difficulty in getting the right class of men to take these positions. I am speaking from the standpoint of the Maritime provinces practically altogether. The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) gave some little account of the way it worked out in Nova Scotia. It is very much the same in New Brunswick. Our Supreme Court in

New Brunswick is divided into two sections, the appellant division consisting of three judges, a chief justice and two puisne judges. Then there is the King's Bench division, which consists of a chief justice and three others. The two chief justices receive $7,000 a year and the others $6,000. The county court judges require just as much knowledge of the law and they must be just as able lawyers as are the judge of the King's Bench division, because exactly the same class of cases is brought within their purview. Under our arrangement civil matters up to $400 in contract and $200 in tort are decided by the county court judges. Beyond that the cases go to the King's Bench. The same amount of legal acumen is required in deciding a case involving an amount of $399 as that which is required in a case involving $400. My hon. friend does not seem to appreciate the fact that as far as the Maritime provinces county court judges are concerned they are exactly on a par with the King's Bench judges, except that they receive half the salary. I think the minister must be alive to the fact that this is an unfair basis. This is a position that these gentlemen ought not to be asked to sustain, and I trust that at an early period my hon. friend will be able to do something to remove this anomaly. Since this discussion commenced this evening I have been casting my eye over the Estimates in every department of the Government in Ottawa, and n you look at these Estimates you will find from one to eight or nine officials outside of the deputy ministers who are receiving salaries greater than those of the county court judges I have nothing to say against these gentlemen; they are doing the work assigned to them, but they are only clerks. I do not think the Minister of Justice can consider for a moment that a chief clerk in a department at Ottawa has anything like the responsibilitty devloving upon him as has a county court judge in the Maritime provinces; the two cases are not comparable.
And these officials are not satisfied.

No doubt they are not
satisfied, but I am only mentioning them as a matter of comparison. In this very building to-night there are eleven or twelve gentlemen, not including the Clerk of the House, the Clerk of the Senate, the Sergeant-at-Arms and important officials of that kind, who are mere clerks and who are
receiving a greater salary than the county court judges in the Maritime provinces. I am not going to say anything about the Militia Department; I had something to say about that last week, but if the Minister of Justice would look at the salaries of the officials of the Militia Department he would be ashamed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would find a good example there.

Yes, you would find all the justification you possibly could require to increase the salary of judges who really are doing something for the country, who are a necessity to the country, and who are earning their salary. Again, I am not attacking the Militia Department; I am only mentioning this by way of comparison If it be necessary to keep this body of military gentlemen in their positions at enormous salaries, surely the Minister of Justice ought to be able to equalize the matter by raising the salaries of the county court judges to somewhat near what they should be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In so far as we have listened to argument upon the general increase of the salaries of county court judges, and perhaps of judges, generally speaking, I have very strong sympathy with that view. The hon. gentleman from Regina (Mr. Martin) said that I was in good humour up in Regina, and that I intimated my feeling in that regard. I may say, as a matter of fact, that on that question I am always in good humour and I always entertain the same feeling. Unfortunately one is not always able to- do these things which in the best of humour he wishes to do.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not alone to deal with this matter, and there are other considerations than those which have been advanced this evening that appear to be paramount obstacles to the general dealing with this subject at this session. It is quite true that I promised to do my best, and I have endeavoured to keep my promise. But the circumstances have not been favourable, and we are not in a position to deal with the whole subject at present. I have explained the peculiar circumstances of what is being done in Quebec. This is not a matter of increasing salaries pure and simple. So far as the Superior Court judges are concerned, we are avoiding the appointing of two addi-

tional judges by making arrangements by which existing judges do considerably more work for a small addition to their (salaries. It is from that point of view that one hon. gentleman has been good enough to speak of it as being, what in reality it is, an economy.
I do not want to go into comparisons' which might seem invidious, but I do know of my personal knowledge the immense volume of work the circuit court judges in Montreal do. The province of Quebec thought there was so much work that there should be six judges in the circuit court, but I have so arranged matters that it is possible to do the work with four judges, and I am simply distributing between these four the six thousand dollars salary that would have been paid to two .additional judges at $3,000 each. I am not in reality burdening the treasury of this country with any addition to the salaries of particular judges. What I am doing with regard to the Superior Court judges who come into the district of Montreal, is, adding two increases of salary of two thousand dollars each, instead of paying salaries for two additional judges at seven tl uusand dollars each. In the case of the Circuit Court judges, I am getting the work done by four men, and paying the same as I would have paid if I simply folded my arms and made no effort, and added two judges at the suggestion of the legislature. I have to acknowledge the cooperation of the Government of the province of Quebec in this arrangement. An hon. member has said that it is for the province to fix the number of the judges, and I have to acknowledge that this arrangement could not have been come to without the co-operation of the Government of the province of Quebec.
As to the statement made by the hon. member for Prince Edward Island (Mr. A.
A. McLean), there is no doubt that the Chief Justice of that province receives less than the Chief Justices of the other provinces, but on the other hand the puisne judges of that province receive more than the rural puisne judges in Quebec. There are anomalies with regard to these salaries, Perhaps it is true that something ought to be done to remedy these anomalies, but they seemed quite satisfactory to a large number of gentlemen who have spoken this evening, at the time they were brought into existence, and so long as it remained in their power to change them. These hon. gentlemen seem to have discovered the great 
need for a change only when their power to make the change slipped from them. But that does not alter the force that attaches to the argument that there ought to be a change, and speaking for myself personally, I shall be glad if circumstances should put me in a position where I shall be free to deal with this whole subject. As I have said, circumstances have not appeared this year to be favourable to that being done, and I regret it as much as any of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken. The hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) touched a sympathetic chord when he spoke of the position of the judges in the district of Montreal. I am as sorry as he can be that we are not in a position to deal with the whole subject, and in dealing with the whole subject to deal with their case. The action that is being taken here now is purely and simply giving effect to an arrangement that enables us, while avoiding a larger burden on the treasury, to get a more effective administration in a particular district. It is not a matter of increasing salaries purely and simply, because for what we are doing we are getting a direct consideration of greater value than we are giving.
Is there any arrangement made with regard to the judge in the district of Gaspe?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I must confess that I know of no reason why the judge in Gaspe should be treated differently from the other rural judges in the province of Quebec.

His salary remains at
$5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Does he reside in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The judge in the county ol Gaspe exercises his functions also in Bonaventure, with residence at New Carlisle or at Perce, at his choice.
That is a requirement of the provincial law, I presume?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
His salary is $5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
He sits in Quebec almost all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That must be because of his own willingness to do so, and it must be remembered that he gets ten dollars a day for expenses when he does so.
Why should not the same arrangement be made in these two other cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the proposition should come from the provincial authorities to make the change, I shall consider what ought to be done; but I do not know the circumstances under which the hon. member says the judge of the district of Gaspe resides in Quebec. His residence apparently by law is fixed in his district.

I am not reflecting on
the judge of the county of Gaspe. He is a distinguished man and has had a very noteworthy career in judicial life, but he occupies the same position as other judges have before him. His immediate predecessor resided at New Carlisle.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
He resides at
Rimouski.

The judge resides there in the summer time, but in Quebec in winter. I understand he sits very often in Quebec. The same thing might apply to the judge at Rimouski. I suppose the same thing applies to other judges who reside in the city of Quebec. The only objection I have is that there should be any discrimination. When a judge is appointed to the Superior Court Bench, he should obtain the same salary as his confreres. Ten, twelve or thirteen years ago Sir Charles Fitzpatrick brought a resolution before the House and by an error, according to his statement, no increases were granted to these judges and it was a source of conplaint for many years after that.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That has been remedied.

I am not blaming the
present Administration, but I think there is a discrimination against these district judges, if the salary remains at $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All the rural judges are on the same basis.

You are taking three rural judges now and making city judges of them. Why not do the same thing with the judges of the district of Gaspe as with the judges of the districts of Richelieu, St. Hyacinthe and Montcalm?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are not all required in the district of Montreal, and it would not be a very practical arrangement that a judge should have a district down in Gaspe and also have a district in Montreal, thus spending a large part of his time travelling between the two places. Where
we have sanctioned this action, it has been in the cases of districts immediately adjoining Montreal, where a man living in Montreal can with equal facility serve his own district and the district of Montreal and because of the need existing in the district of Montreal, and the possibility of its being done with perfect convenience and without loss of time, we have sanctioned the arrangement with regard to these particular judges. Of course, we do not require all the rural judges in the district of Montreal, and we are beginning with those whose districts are nearest to the district of Montreal.

I am not objecting to the arrangement at all, but I think it might be extended to the other parts of the province. Gaspe may seem very remote, but it is now within a few hours of the city of Quebec.
I think that no discrimination should be made between judges occupying equal rank and doing equal work. If in their own districts the work is not sufficient, the Government should give them additional work, if possible, instead of increasing the number of judges. So far as the Circuit Court judges are concerned, I have the pleasure of knowing these judges from the day they were appointed. Three of them were originally appointed, and now the number has been increased to four; but our friends in the Maritime provinces may not know that last year there were before this court 18,000 cases to be tried, and because the role was so overcrowded, two judges of the Superior Court had to be appointed to assist these judges in catching up in their work. The court is presided over by Mr. Justice Leboeuf, who is certainly a very hardworking man and who is entitled to get all he is receiving, and the other judges are Mr. Justice Purcell and by Mr. Justice Dorion, of whom the same is true. I do not believe on the whole that the people of the province will object to reasonable salaries being given the judges, but I do not think discrimination is in the interest of justice. Instead of employing additional judges, the present judges should be given the work, but they should at the same time receive the salary.

I see that as regards
these judges who are to be appointed for the district of Quebec, Chicoutimi or RobeT-val are the places of residence. Where will they reside?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provision of the
Quebec statute is that the judge in the

district of Chicoutimi, shall reside at Roberval, or Chicoutimi, at his choice.

Is there any provision in the statute by which the Minister of Justice can compel a rural judge to reside in his district? If so, is it the intention of the minister to enforce the law so far as the rural judges are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The residence of a judge in the province of Quebec is fixed by the legislation of the province of Quebec. In what manner the Minister of Justice could exercise compulsion upon a judge to obey the law of the province, is perhaps a matter that might require some consideration. So far I have not had called to my attention a case or cases calling for action in that regard.

The best way to enforce
the law would be to stop the salary unless the judge complied with the provincial law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are talking about
judges of the Superior Court of Quebec, and the only remedy of which I know, exercisable against judges of the Superior Court is impeachment before both Houses of Parliament. Whether it would be considered a case for impeachment that a gentleman was residing in one place rather than in another is a . matter which requires some reflection. Short of that I do not know of any authority that the minister has to compel a judge actually to sit down and stay in a particular place. I am not prepared to say that there is nothing that can be done under these circumstances. When such a case arises and is called to my attention, I shall look into the matter and see whether or not it is possible that something can be done to ensure that a judge performs the duty that the provincial law prescribes for him of residing in a particular place. It is not something incumbent upon him under the law of the Dominion of Canada, and therefore it may perhaps not be our function to compel obedience to that law.

The legislature fixes a
district and it assigns the place of residence of the judges. Then, the federal authority provides the salary. I submit, the federal Parliament could impose conditions on the payment of these salaries. It could provide that the judge shall comply with the law made by the provincial legislature, and otherwise shall not be entitled to receive the salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is possible, and
if the case arises we will see.

Will the minister tell
me whether or not he considers that one of his judges has the right to remain in the active command of the unit of the militia. The question might arise as to whether he might be called upon to order out the militia in the case of riot or disturbance. Has that matter been brought to the minister's attention?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is asking for an opinion which turns on the interpretation of a section of the statute. In that case. I am sure he will allow me time to give the subject consideration. The only provision I recall that could be suggested as applicable is that which prohibits a judge from engaging in any other occupation and requires that he shall give his whole time to the duties of his office. I doubt whether service in the militia would be held as going into an * occupation ' within the meaning of the statute. When the case arises we will consider what the law is.

I desire to call the attention of the minister to an anomaly that exists in the County Court Judges' Act in respect to the travel and living allowance to county court judges who have to hold court in places other than the shire town of the county in which they reside. No provision appears to exist for payment of such an allowance when the judge has to travel from one town to another in his home county for the purpose of holding court. I called the attention of the minister to this matter before, and he suggested that I send him a memorandum with respect to it. This I did and I hope he will bear it in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I received the hon.
gentleman's memorandum and will endeavour to see what can be done.
Can it be done without legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not quite recall.
I understand it is somewhat similar to the difficulty spoken of by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). The difficulty of which hs spoke, I understood, arose under some regulation of the department, but the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), refers to the County Court Judges' Act. Do I understand that is a provision of our own Judges' Act?
It is a provision under the Dominion statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will look into it, and when we come to deal with the Bill to carry out this resolution, if necessary I will see that an amendment is made to meet the case.

The case is where a
judge is presiding over two or three counties. As the law now stands the judge can get no travelling fees for attending courts in the county where he resides. This is a matter of considerable hardship and there is no reason why this anomaly should exist. I trust that before this Bill becomes law the minister will see that it is amended to meet such eases as I have referred to.

The minister said that there were no complaints to his department about judges not residing in their districts. I wish to call his attention to the fact that in the district of Kamouraska the complaint is that the judge should resi'de at Fraserville, the shire town of the district. If I may rely upon what the newspapers in that district state, then it is against the best interests of justice in that district to have a judge who does not reside at the shire town. It is within my own knowledge that the judge was obliged to go away earlier than was expected to Quebec, and some witnesses were sent back to their homes and were obliged to come back at the next term at a cost of over $250-an expense uselessly caused by the fact that the judge had to go to another case at Quebec. If the hon. minister has no complaint from that district, I profit by the circumstance to be the first man to lay the complaint before him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman tell me where the residence of that judge is fixed? I notice that in the Quebec statute, with regard to the district of Kamouraska, the provision is that the judge shall reside ' at the place assigned to him by law.' And I understand that under the Quebec law, that means that the Lieutenant Governor in Council may fix the judge's place of residence. . I will verify that if the hon. member is not able to tell me what action has been taken.

Judge Cimon nearly always lived at Rivi&re du Loup for the best interests of justice. He has been replaced by Mr. Justice Belleau, and it is all changed since Judge Cimon is gone.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. DOHERTY thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 190, to amend the Judges' Act.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
